speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
House again in Committee on Bill (No. 128), to authorize a loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific.-Mr. Fielding.
On the preamble.

I asked several questions of the Minister of Finance when we were last in committee, and he said he would endeavour to get the information. I asked whether the $205,000 which is mentioned as having been paid on the Grand Trunk Pacific stock went into the actual construction

of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and how it was paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
While reference was made in the debate to a number of points,
I do not recall that any specific question was put on which I was expected to procure additional statements, hut I shall have the matter looked into further.

Several questions were asked about the $9,000,000 said to have been invested in the railway by the Grand Trunk Pacific, and whether that included the $9,000,000 invested in equipment or rolling stock? The minister was not sure, but he was of the opinion that the rolling stock could only be provided for by an issue of equipment bonds, and that, therefore, it could not be called an investment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not understand I was to get further information. I gave my hon. friend the information I had, and thought with that he was content; that is to say, that the rolling stock was provided by an issue of equipment bonds, and that, therefore, it could not refer to the item which he mentioned. The chief engineer of the government informs me that is his idea of the matter also. I would not consider that an investment by the company of the company's funds; it is an investment by the people who purchased the bonds.

Then, the $9,000,000 would be the amount of money invested by the Grand Trunk Pacific in the construction of the road. Does that $9,000,000 invested in the construction of the road include the advance of the Grand Trunk Pacific of more than $7,000,000, and when this Bill is passed and the loan got, and the Grand Trunk is repaid by the Grand Trunk Pacific, will the Grand Trunk Pacific then have $9,000,000 of an investment, or will it own $9,000,000 minus this $7,000,000, which may be simply in there as an advance they have got from the Grand Trunk? It makes a great deal of difference. We want to know what this Grand Trunk Pacific, with its moneyed men, its immense influence and its great resources, has actually put into this road, and we do not know that at present.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not understand that the Grand Trunk corporation-we are not dealing with individuals, but with the corporation-are expected to put in, out of the Grand Trunk treasury, a single dollar. What they agreed to do was to guarantee the Grand Trunk Pacific Company's bonds, to assist the subsidiary company in raising money. If they have in the meantime advanced any money out of their treasury, as would seem to be indicated by the papers, I would regard that as a temporary advance, and not as a contribution
of the Grand Trunk to the enterprise. All the Grand Trunk agreed to do was to guarantee the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, within certain limitations. That is what they have been doing, that is what they are still doing under this legislation, and therefore, I would not consider that in the sense I understand my hon. friend's question, they have contemplated any investment at all.
The investment they are to make is not an investment of funds of the treasury of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. It is the credit of the Grand Trunk Company which they pledge by way of guarantee, and the proceeds of that guarantee go into the railway. I do not understand that the Grand Trunk Railway Company ever intend or propose to aid the railway in any other way.

The Finance Minister has hardly caught the drift of my question. We have incorporated the Grand Trunk Pacific Company-I am not now talking of the Grand Trunk Company at all; they have their directors, their shareholders, their influence. The statement is made that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company have invested $9,000,000. Now what I wanted to know is whether they have invested $9,000,000 outside of the advance which the Grand Trunk Railway Company made to them of over $7,000,000, or if, when this loan Bill is passed, and when the money is paid over to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and the Grand Trunk Company gets back its advance of $7,000,000, the minister will be able to say that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company has invested $9,000,000 in it, or whether he will have to say that they have invested $9,000,000 minus this advance which they will have paid back to the Grand Trunk Railway Company; that is, will their investment then be $9,000,000 or less.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The investment of which company? .
Of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not understand that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company have any $9,000,000 invested except the money that was raised by issue of public securities. Certainly I have had no such understanding.
The Minister's answer says that the Grand Trunk Pacific have invested $9,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, I think not. I think the investment my hon. friend mentions must refer to the Grand Trunk Company itself and not to the Grand Trunk

Pacific Company. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company moneys are derived almost entirely, except as respects a moderate sum, from the issue of public securities, one set being guaranteed by the Dominion and one set by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. I do not understand there are any other funds available. My hon. friends opposite asked a number of questions which did not seem to me to be of very great importance; nevertheless I have brought down the information as desired. I do not in every case admit that it is essential to the discussion of this question, but I thought it desirable to meet so far as I could the questions of my hon. friend. I think he will find that it has relation to the investment of the Grand Trunk Company. But I have sent for my officer, and I will have the papers in a moment.
The company, as I understand it, is the National Transcontinental Railway Company, and the answers must be_ in reference to that company. I find in this statement one of the answers is as follows:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Is that an answer to one of the questions asked?

No, not in this case. But there was a question on the Order Paper, and those two answers were given. There is an answer about the investment of rolling stock; the amount expended in rolling stock by the Grand Trunk Pacific was said to be $8,273,000. But I am quite certain that the question with reference to the total investment was as to the investment of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. I am quoting now the answer to one of these questions from the statement brought down by the minister on page 2. Now, the minister says that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company has made no investment in it. Money has been raised for the Grand Trunk Pacific Company and paid over to that company, and that becomes the Grand Trunk Pacific Company's investment, though raised by bonds guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Company. They are primarily Grand Trunk Pacific bonds, they are therefore Grand Trunk Pacific bonds when guaranteed after they have on them the endorsement of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and when the bonds are transmuted into cash it is the cash of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, and therefore it is an investment of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I want to know whether the $9,000,000 the minister said the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company had invested, includes the advance of the $7,000,000 made to them by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which advance has been paid back.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: The question was asked by the leader of the opposition and answered by the minister. I find it quoted on page 5406 of the ' Hansard ' by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middlebro):

In reply to a question put by the leader of the opposition the following answer was given by the government :-
The company state that the total amount invested bv the promoters in the undertaking is $9,597,149, and that the total amount invested in the rolling stock is $8,273,454.
Now, what I desired to know was whether that $9,597,149 invested by the promoters in the undertaking includes the advance of over $7,000,000 made by the Grand Trunk Railway. I imagine that it does.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The question is; Does the $9,700,000 odd include the $7,000,000 advanced by the Grand Trunk Company? I understand that it does. Now, on the rolling stock I desire to confirm my previous statement that the rolling stock is purchased by a separate issue of bonds, and I do not understand that it is referred to in that item at all.

That is what I took it to be. We have that answered satisfactorily.

Now, can the minister give me any more satisfaction than he has heretofore as to the amount invested in the rolling stock, which is $8,273,000? That is raised by equipment bonds and that is the rolling stock which has been loaned or leased to the Grand Trunk on the conditions which have been named? I suppose that is a fact?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. My hon. friend's present question relates entirely to the rolling stock?
Yes.	.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: That is satisfactory. Now, if the minister can tell me equally satisfactorily how that $205,000 is got at I would be very glad. I understood before that there are certain directors who got a certain amount of stock and paid up a small percentage upon it-$5,000 odd being the total amount paid, while $249,000 worth of shares stands in the name of Smithers and some others. I suppose that is held in trust?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

The statement is made somewhere that on that $205,000 has been paid. How has that $205,000 been paid? Has any portion of the stock been sold or has any portion of it been given as security on which $205,000 has been raised? How has the $205,000 been got and once it was got where did it go to?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I find that my officer has asked one of the officers of the company for information which would enable us to answer that as far as possible and that he has not received their Teply. I would hope to have it during the day.

May I ask the Finance Minister if he can supply the committee, either to-day,, or at some early day, with a list of the directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, of the Grand Trunk Railway Company and of the other companies that are connected with this undertaking? There are four or five companies.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It would help me very much to get the information if the hon. gentleman would kindly enumerate the companies the names of whose directors he desires to know. As to the directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific we have that information before us. The names of the directors of the Grand Trunk Railway Company can easily be found. There was an annual meeting a few days ago and the directors were chosen. I could get it from the public press if my hon. friend has not seen it. What others does he desire?
The Grand Trunk Pacific Townsite Company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am informed that information has already been given in the House in answer to a question. The directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific Townsite Company are Chas. M. Hays, E. J. Chamberlin, Wm. Wainwright, W. H. Biggar and E. H. Fitzhugh. These are all officials of the Grand Trunk Railway Company.
Now the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I presume the Act incorporating them would give the provisional directors. I really do not know what steps have been taken in that respect. If my hon. friend regards it as important I w'ill ask the company to give the names of the directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company. I would expect to find these companies composed of the principal officials of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Are there any other companies in regard to which my hon. friend desires information?
Yes, the Grand Trunk Pacific Construction Company, -whose directors are members of the Grand Trunk Railway Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I will be glad to get them, but I am sure my hon. friend will find that they are composed of the principal officials of the Grand Trunk Railway.
We also desire to know who are the directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific Telegraph Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All right.
I suppose we might expect to have these names brought down before the third reading of the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If I do not get the information before the third reading I will promise to give it to my hon. friend afterwards. I do not suppose the point is of sufficient importance to delay the measure.
No.

If there are any other Grand Trunk Pacific companies my

hon. friend the Minister of Finance might bring down the names of the directors of these companies as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am afraid my hon. friend will have to give me the names.

I do not clearly understand the financing of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway as stated by the Minister of Finance. All the assets of the Grand Trunk Pacific, as I understand it, must be derived from the sale of bonds or stock. The total amount that has been realized and belongs to the Grand Trunk Pacific, according to the returns brought down, is about $9,000,000. The sale of the bonds alone amounts to nearly $9,000,000. How could the $9,000,000 include the $7,000,000 which is owing to the Grand Trunk Railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The seven million dollars do not represent bonds.
I understand that perfectly well. The $9,000,000 includes, the minister states, $7,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.
If it includes the $7,000,000 the Grand Trunk Pacific do not get credit for the amount of bonds they have sold.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a separate account.
But you say they are the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have given my hon. friend the particulars of it.
Yes, but I cannot understand it. The whole of the assets of the Grand Trunk Pacific must come either from the sale of stock or of bonds?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Surely.

The total amount realized by the sale of bonds amounted to about $9,000,000. The amount sold for the purpose of building the prairie section and a part of the mountain section realized in the neighbourhood of $9,000,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. for one section.

Then the total amount that the Grand Trunk Pacific have put into the construction must be the amount of bonds they have sold, plus the amount that they got from the sale of stock, which is a small amount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend is mistaken; there are two sums mentioned in these papers which each happen to be about $9,000,000 but they are not the same sum at all. The $9,000,000 referred to under the issue of bonds is shown on the first page and it certainly does not represent the same sum as the $9,000,000 shown farther on. They are two different things although they happen to be about the same amount of money.

That brings us to another query. What other resources has the Grand Trunk Pacific out of which it has realized $2,000,000? If the $9,500,000 are investments of the Grand Trunk Pacific, not including the proceeds of the bonds, and if the $9,500,000 include the $7,000,000 of an advance, that means that $2,500,000 have been invested by the promoters and that this money has been got from some other source. What other source?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I would naturally assume it was got by borrowing on the credit of the Grand Trunk Pacific for the various forms of its work. That is the most natural explanation. It is an investment in the sense that the company has raised the money and owes it. We know that they have no sources for deriving money except those mentioned by the member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart) but in the meantime, like any other business enterprise, can raise money through banks and financial arrangements.

Does it seem reasonable that the Grand Trunk Pacific, having no securities, has been able to raise $2,500,000 as a loan? What securities can it give? Is that also an advance from the Grand Trunk Railway which has to be paid out of the $10,000,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The information, of course is not in the possession of the government; it had to be obtained from the company. As we were not asked to crossexamine them and find out the details which my hon. friend asks, I am not able to give the information. I give my hon. friend my own impression of how they would raise it, by the ordinary commercial methods.
Bill reported.
Mr. FIELDING moved the third reading of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is shown in the information.
Yes, but the minister stated, in answer to my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster), that the $9,000,000 of bonds includes the $7,000,000. It cannot possibly include it.

Before the Bill is read the third time I desire to make a few remarks, not having said much on the Bill during its progress through committee but having tried from close attention to the questions and answers to find out from the government the exact position of affairs. It seems

to me, speaking generally, that the government shelters itself in certain ways from criticism in this House and in the country. It shelters itself first behind the name of a Transcontinental Railway and in answer to criticisms of great expense or any cognate criticism it simply gives the general answer:	'Oh, we are engaged in
building a great transcontinental railway.' That appeals to the imagination of the people and stifles the proper voice of the people and to a certain extent their criticism as to the ways and means by which the Transcontinental Railway is being built. Then again, I think the government shelters itself behind what they call the ' on all-fours ' position with the loan made to the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1883 and 1884. It needs nothing but a mere statement of the facts to show that there is no all-fours comparison between the loan made to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway in the year 1908-9 and the loan made to the Canadian Pacific Railway in the year 1883-4. Not only is there no parallel in the conditions prevailing then and now, but there is no parallel between the securities that were given by the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1884 and the securities given by the Grand Trunk Pacific in 1909. It seems sufficient to say:	'Oh, the Conservatives
made a loan of $30,000,000 to the Canadian Pacific Railway and we are only making a loan of $10,000,000 to the Grand Trunk Pacific.' That disarms criticism and shuts the mouth willing to be shut, of the partisan, and confounds to a certain extent the criticisms of the man who is not a partisan. Then the government shields itself behind the argument of national necessity. The Minister of Railways took a leaf in a humble way, from the book of the Prime Minister in 1903 and in 1909 he urged as a condonation of the offence, if offence it be, that there was a great national necessity. He even went so far as to employ the argument made by an hon. gentleman in this House not long ago that it was an instrument of national defence. I think some one in the House calculated the $180,000,000 of our country's contribution to this road, divided it by ten and came to the conclusion that it is equal to building eight-teen ' Dreadnoughts ' and putting them on the North sea as a first line of defence, against any attacks that might be made on British supremacy.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

So the Minister of Railways at this late hour revamped the argument of the necessity of this road on the ground of defence. I think it well to let in a little light on that. I suppose that if a line of railway is to be of value as a means of defence it must be from some pre-eminent conditions inherent in it which
are not inherent in the lines we now have. Let us see what these are? In the first place, the Grand Trunk Pacific road commences at Halifax, at St. John or at Moncton, as you please. It passes again at Quebec, if you please; it touches the great city of Winnipeg and then goes to Edmonton, and so through. If a road is to be of value as a line of defence it must be partly because it possesses some advantages in the way of the seaports with which it connects, but the very same seaports of Halifax, St. John and Quebec and a similar seaport on the Pacific coast, in a similar condition of lack of defence or ability for defence, are connected by the Intercolonial, the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern. These railways in their branches and connections commence at the same ports on the Atlantic and end at similar undefended ports upon the western shore. Then a railway might have value as a means of defence, owing to its being situated in the interior of the country, remote from the frontier. If the minister will take the outline map of the Grand Trunk Pacific he will find that it is not the northernmost railway, that from Moncton to Quebec the Intercolonial lies further north than west of Winnipeg, the Canadian Northern is really the railway which goes farthest north, so that whichever way you look at it, as a line of defence there is no force in the argument of the Minister of Railways that it is of sufficient national value to justify this House in criticising it lightly, or to lead the people to bear the burden of this heavy debt without repining. But the great defence of the government and their followers is silence. No matter what criticism is made, they meet it by silence or calling: Carried. No matter what extravagance is shown, they meet it by silence or crying: Carried-the more active ones being the ones who cry: Carried. No matter wbat argument is .advanced with reference to the carrying out of the project, they meet it by utter and absolute silence. Show the Prime Minister that the statement he made in 1903 was as absolutely outside of the mark as a statement could be, he meets it with silence. There is not even the poor penance of repentance, even although it be tardv. made by the minister who deceived this House in 1903 and 1904 by making a representation of conditions which have been proved to be absolutely unreliable. And so silence in the last is the resort. But the Prime Minister and the government must believe themselves that in respect to all these things it is the duty of the opposition and of the country to criticise the methods by which this great scheme has been put on to the country, the methods by which it has been carried on and the

ultimate result which we see in part now, but only in part, which every year reveals to us as something more grievous, more burdensome and more menacing. Thus the duty of the House and the country is not to be misled by the glamour of a great railway or statements as to lines of defence and the like of that, their duty is not to be diverted from the proper and healthy and sane criticism of the methods by which it was conceived and the methods by which it has been carried on, and the ruinous result in some respects in the ultimate fulfilment of the project.
Let me draw the attention of the government and of the House to one thing. Suppose that in 1903 the government, or the Prime Minister representing it, had stated to the House the whole facts of the case as they are to-day deployed in the public light and a matter of record. Does my hon. friend the Prime Minister think that the country would have taken that scheme from him at that time and would have put it through? If the Prime Minister had stated at that time that a simple business proposition had been made to him and this government to aid the construction to a reasonable extent of a railway from the Great Lakes up to Winnipeg and out through a portion of the Northwest, already more or less settled and more or less served by existing and constructing railways, and if he had stated all the facts connected with the scheme which he introduced, the difficulties to be overcome, the unproductive nature of a large portion of the district to be traversed, would he have received the acclaim of the House and the support of the country? I do not think he can convince himself that this would have been the case. The fact is simply this: The first statement of a proposition is apt to carry the mind of the country. Once that is made and the country fully imbued with that statement, you can afterwards undermine that first statement until there is scarcely a vestige of the original scheme left and you [DOT] cannot overtake the first impression that was made. It was under the glamour of that first impression that the Prime Minister carried his scheme. Neither this parliament nor the country would have given adhesion to it if he had stated it in all its bare nakedness in 1903 and 1904 when he brought this proposition before the House. Would he have received support if he had stated, for instance, not only that a business proposition had been made to him which could have been carried out with the minimum of public investment and with but a small amount of obligation by the country, which would have done everything that this costly project has done or can do for many years? Would he have received support if he had Mr. FOSTER.
said in addition that although some man might rise and declare that $13,000,000 would measure the amount the country would have to expend, he must dissent from that statement as being 300 per cent too small? Here is the Prime Minister's own statement on that point:
The sum total of the money to he paid by the government for the construction of the line from .Monoton to the Pacific will be in the neighbourhood of twelve millions of dollars or thirteen millions of dollars and not a cent more.
He went to the country with that statement and he meant that statement to go to the country for in the hand-book of the Liberal party, on which they ran the elections of 1904, we find:
A Transcontinental Railway for $13,000,000.
And in the text this authorized publication says:
It is an actual fact, an indisputable fact, that $13,000,000 will cover every cent of the country's expenditure in connection with the railway.
That is the statement made first by the responsible minister to the House, and made known by the minister's assent to the country on the eve of a general election, in each case positive, in neither case qualified, in each case an absolute pledge to the country that that road would be built and cost the country not one cent more than $13,000,000. Suppose that the Prime Minister in 1903 had said:	'Any
man who says that it would cost this country only $13,000,000 to build this road is either a lunatic or an ignorant man; it will cost this country before we are through with it, not $13,000,000 but $180,000,000 or $200,000,000; if the man's statement is that this $13,000,000 will not be the whole advance and amount but only the balance of cash that the country will have to pay, it is equally absurd, for the balance the country will put up in the end will be nearer $50,000,000 than' $13,000,000.' Suppose that the Prime Minister had stated that in 1903, would he have been able to put his scheme through as easily? But look at it again. In support of this scheme the Prime Minister took an unusual course; he went behind the responsible Minister of Railways, he hatched this scheme without the knowledge of that minister. After it had been hatched and the chicken was able to run about and make itself visible, it was introduced to the notice of the then Minister of Railways (Mr. Blair), whereupon that minister declared that the product was too costly, that the undertaking would cost this country $139,000,000, and he took the course-the course of a man who knew his responsibility as Minister of Railways in my right hon. friend's cabinet-of resigning from the cabinet and

going back to his seat as a private member. If the Prime Minister had not deceived the House at that time, if he had made it apparent as his Minister of Railways did, that this scheme would cost $139,000,000 at least, would he have got his scheme through so easily?
My right hon. friend had another argument. He declared that this country was under the imminency of dire peril. The United States, our powerful neighbour to the South, were threatening us, he said, with the extinction of the bonding system. We were not safe, and he prayed God that we might not have delayed too long in taking action, because even then, we had delayed almost too long. If he had stated what he knew to be the truth that there was not the slightest vestige in existence of any threat or menace from the United States in that respect, and no ground for our anticipating any national peril or calamity from that quarter, he would have been lacking in another of his strong arguments in favour of his scheme.
Another plea which he made use of was that it would open up a new route through our rich prairie regions in the Northwest, He said this knowing quite well or he should have known the contrary to be the case. There can be no doubt about his having used that argument. The impression he left, the impression he meant to leave, on the members of this House, the impression he intended to create in the country, was that this railway would give us an entrance into an undeveloped portion of our great heritage in the Northwest and open to settlement an immense area of virgin territory. But if he had told the truth, he would have told parliament and the country that that railway, starting from Winnipeg, lay in and out along the lines of existing railways, for every mile of its course, until it reaches Battle river. But in that case, he would not have got through his scheme on the glamour created by this prospect of opening up a new great prairie region. Take the map lately published by the Railway Department, take the railway map issued by the Department of the Interior, and follow the course of this railway after it touches Winnipeg. When it goes into the Northwest from Winnipeg, it runs thence to Portage la Prairie, from Portage to Saskatoon, and from Saskatoon to Battle river and along every mile it is cheek by jowl with railways already built. It is not the opener up of a new country. The road which opens up the new7 country north of the River Saskatchewan is the Canadian Northern. But the statement of the Prime Minister was that we were undertaking this burden in order to open up a new zone in the Northwest. My right hon. friend cannot shelter himself behind the statement that this railway scheme of his has opened
up a new country in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. It was not launched on that ground. The main thing it was to do was to open up new territory to provide homes for thousands of new settlers in the west. Its main object was to open up new wheat fields in remote and unutilized portions of our western territories, which would contribute to the wealth, progress, and prosperity of this country. But had he stated exactly what was going to hanpen, he would have been bereft of that very strong position wdiich he took before the House and the country.
So much with reference to the inception of the scheme. But when we come to its working out, let us look at the Laurier work in that respect. All through the late campaign the cry raised by the right hon. gentleman's supporters was that Laurier should be allowed to finish his work. What was that work? It was the construction of a National Transcontinental Railway. That was the monument which my right hon. friend was building for himself and which he desired to finish. Let us then look at the work of the right hon. gentleman, not only in its inception, but in its carrying out. I have shown that every bit of the edifice built so far is built upon a false foundation. Let us come now to the working out of his scheme. My right hon. friend told this House and the country over and over again that the liability of Canada would be protected, that the advances of Canada would be secured, and that the security would be a first guarantee upon the undertaking. That was to be one of the first things provided for in the legislative work. To a certain extent that was provided for in the first contract. But the first contract was not signed by the Grand Trunk Pacific. It was signed only by the government; and in 1904 the chief work of my right hon. friend, the builder of this great monument, was to undermine and lessen the securities of Canada for her advances and increase the advances she was to make. There can be no doubt about that. The first mortgage we were to have had was entirely taken out. The second mortgage is now on a parity with the first. The preference of the first mortgagee was entirely eliminated from the Bill, yet my right hon. friend had gained the support of the House and the country on the ground that we were to be protected as first mortgagee and not as second. What ' was done? Our liabilities were raised by subsequent legislation. At first we were only to guarantee three-quarters of the actual cost in the mountains beyond the prairies, and that actual cost was limited by a maximum sum, but the legislation introduced later raised our liabilities to three-quarters of the actual cost, unlimited by any maximum sum, with the exception of the prairie section. It raised our liabilities by millions of dollars in both the prairie

and mountain sections as well. Not only were they raised in that way, but in addition, the rights we had as first mortgagee were postponed and depreciated until they became virtually of no effect. Under the legislation, as it exists to-day, this is the condition of Canada. In the first place we pay interest on the mountain section for seven years. In the second place, the Grand Trunk Pacific can make default of interest three years after that seven years have expired, and that can be capitalized and added to their indebtedness. That makes ten years, and then, after that ten years is over, they have a period of five years during which, if they are in default, we cannot take over the road. The only recourse we have is to put in a manager to administer it; and if there be not sufficient income to pay for the management, the people have to foot the deficit. We can put in a receiver, it is inconceivable that we can allow that road to stop, and if the income be not sufficient to operate it, who pays the difference? The Dominion government. It is the people who are responsible. But if it should pay a surplus, then we have to divide that surplus between ourselves and the Grand Trunk Railway bond-holders. If it should become paying, then our receiver hands it back to the Grand Trunk Pacific. And so on ad infinitum until every vestige of our rights as mortgagee has passed away entirely under the constructive policy in the legislative line of my right hon. friend the Prime Minster. Every step of that policy adds to the responsibility of Canada and takes away from the security which Canada in the first instance had. Again, by the legislation of my right hon. friend, we are bound to build the eastern section, and when we had built that section, professedly in connection with one great transcontinental line, that legislation failed to provide that the Grand Trunk Pacific should lease that eastern section which we built. And I contend to-day, as I have always done, that if after this eastern section is built, the Grand Trunk Pacific do not choose to exercise their option of leasing and operating the road and paying us three per cent on its cost, there is no power in that legislation to compel the Grand Trunk Pacific to exercise its option and to enter into a lease of that eastern section or any part of it. They are given the option to take out any portion they please and run that portion and leave any portion they please. That is the position in which my right hon. friend, in his constructive work as a legislator, has left this country after we have built the eastern section from Winnipeg to Moncton.
Let us go a step further. If the right hon. gentleman was strong in anything, he was strong, in his inception of the legislation and in his canvass before the country on this point, that what he wanted to do Mr. FOSTER.
was to open up the Northwest and bring the great traffic of the country down through Canadian channels to our own seaports. That was a good drawing card. That was a very mesmeric policy to lay before the people. We have been spending many of our precious millions on east and west lines of communication with the idea of ultimately building up our seaports and our Canadian merchant marine; and my right hon. friend said to the House and the country: 'Here is a scheme by which we propose to tap the great Northwest and bring its rich products through Canadian channels and through Canadian seaports, to the benefit of our own people and our Canadian marine/ He there stuck a good cord which sounded sweet music to the people. But how has he carried that policy out? Why, he absolutely refused to complete that idea by the legislation necessary. Although this side of the House urged him to do so, he brought his political support to the point of refusing any legislation which would make it certain that that stated prin-cinle, upon which he founded his scheme and the immense burden the country was to assume in regard to it, would be fairly carried out. What happened? Fie entered into a contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific that, with the exception of freight routed by the shippers of their own stuff, the Grand Trunk Pacific was, to the best of its ability, to see that western freight should go through Canadian channels and Canadian ports. But then what happened? No provision was made to meet the very important position taken by the Grand Trunk Railway. The Grand Trunk Railway taps the Grand Trunk Pacific at the junction north of Lake Superior 220 miles. Every ounce of freight which is gathered up in the Northwest and which is unrouted when it comes down to Lake Superior junction, goes directly over the Grand Trunk Railway tu that company's terminals, and ports, on the lakes. Every ounce of it. The moment it leaves the Grand Trunk Pacific line and goes into the transportation system of the Grand Trunk Railway, the Grand Trunk Pacific is not of the slightest account as regards ' the direction of that traffic. There is no provision against that in the present legislation. Will my right hon. friend hazard, in the light of his preceding statements, the further assertion that in" the years to come the greater part of the products of the Northwest will go over * the Grand Trunk Pacific system on its long overland route through the north of Ontario and the north of Quebec and the portion of New Brunswick which it traverses? Will he hazard the statement that such products will take that route? Will it not, on the contrary, the moment it reaches the Lake Superior junction, take the short cut off to the water,

and thereafter be in the hands of and at the will of freight carriers over whom we have no influence whatever. The Prime Minister was asked by us to make good his original proposition by binding the Grand Trunk Railway under the same conditions as the Grand Trunk Pacific, so that when the Grand Trunk Railway received its rich freights from the west at Lake Superior junction, it should be bound to send all, except the routed freights, through Canadian channels to Canadian ports. He refused to do this. This year he was given another opportunity to do the same thing. This year he is granting a favour to the Grand Trunk Railway. The Grand Trunk Railway, according to his statement, was to receive $25,000,000 as capital stock from the Grand Trunk Pacific. According to his statement, that stock was to be used for the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific, so that when the Grand Trunk Pacific wanted money, it could call upon the proceeds of that stock at par for the money it needed.
My right hon. friend stated that, he adhered to that, he went to the country on that, and got his election on that, in connection with other things. Now he comes into the House, and his Finance Minister states in so many plain words: 'Not a dollar of that stock need be called upon, or ought in equity to be called upon, to supply money to build the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway; that stock belongs to the Grand Trunk Railway, and is a payment for guaranteeing the bonds which, under contract, it has agreed to guarantee.' Now what can be made of a position so diametrically opposed to the position of pre election times? And what becomes of the solemn statement of the Prime Minister when, a few years afterwards, he has the absolute contradiction made to it by his own Finance Minister, and he himself by his legislation coincides with that contradiction of the Finance Minister? So that to-day he is doing for the Grand Trunk Railway a favour by becoming their banker, under that condition of things loading up the country with $10,000,000 more, because he. repeatedly stated in this House that we would not be called upon for another cent, that the Grand Trunk Railway was a responsible company, the Grand Trunk Railway got the stock, and got it for the purpose of financial aid, and our liabilities were limited by the contract, and whatever other money was necessary would have to be provided by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which was able, responsible and bound by the contract to carry it out. Today he nullifies his statement by his legislation, he loads the country in the interest of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Now when he comes to-dav with a favour to the Grand Trunk Railway Company,
and is asked again:	'Will you put in a
clause now by which the Grand Trunk Railway Company will be bound to forward all unrouted freight through Canadian channels and through Canadian seaports,' what is the answer of my right hon. friend? Mr. Speaker, will I be out of order if I say, a quibble, and nothing better than a quibble? He says, 'Oh, this is not the time to do it.' Is it not a time at which it could be done? Are we not doing a favour to the Grand Trunk Railway Company over and above everything we were bound to do? When a $10,000,000 loan is made as a favour, when the invitation is held out to the same company, by the Minister of Railways and Canals and by the Minister of Finance: 'Come again next, year if you are in difficulties, and we will do the same,' is it not an opportune time when, if my hon. friend were honest in his desire to assure the passage of the great west products through Canadian territory and out of Canadian ports, he could make that certain in the only way in which he could make it certain? But he will not do it, this is not the opportunity.
Then he went one step beyond what was necessary, a case of a witness volunteering more than the simple answer to his question, and he said, 'There will be an opportunity.' When? When the lease is made by the Grand Trunk Pacific for the entire portion of the eastern section. But when a lease is made for the entire portion of the eastern section, with whom is that lease made ? With the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and not with the Grand Trunk Railway Company. And though you duplicate the present arrangement when you make that lease with the Grand Trunk Pacific, what power have you got over the distributor of this freight, which is the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself? So he knew, if he knew the- law, that when that opportunity came he would be absolutely powerless to tack on any condition binding the Grand Trunk Railway Company. He will be making a lease with the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the only thing he could do would be to try to modify their contract. But their contract is plain in that respect now, and he could not make it any stronger than it is at present. So that an apparent answer was really deceptive to the people of this country and to the House. That is the condition in which we are today, and to-day I charge upon the right hon. gentleman that his main argument that the rich products of the west should be directed through our own seaports and our own Canadian channels, is not guarded or guaranteed by any- legislation to that effect, and the right hon. gentleman refuses to guarantee it, now when he has the op-

portunity of his life for attaching a condition to the great favour we are giving to the Grand Trunk Railway Company.
Let me go a step farther and let me ask my right hon. friend, as he has been asked by the leader of the opposition, to view the situation of things in the east, and my right hon. friend did not deign to answer. It was put up to him as specifically, as categorically, as any man could put it. What did he propose to do in view of the condition of things in the east, with the Quebec bridge nowhere, not to be finished until 1915, a part of the eastern section almost entirely built, and which will be finished within a year's time-what did he propose to do in that condition of things? What was my right hon. friend's answer? 'It must not surprise the House,' he said, 'if I inform them that I and my colleagues have been thinking that matter over.' Well, perhaps it might not surprise the unthinking portion of the House, but even that might surprise some of the members in the House who are cognizant of the haphazard way in which my right hon. Iriend entered into this great scheme, and into cognate schemes in reference to it. He has been considering it. But when he came to give a definite idea as to what would be done, the right hon. gentleman had not an idea; he simply said, 'I do not know what can be done; somebody has mentioned a ferry-' and he stopped there. Nobody had mentioned anything else, but somebody had mentioned a ferry, but he did not know what could be done about it, and in the end he took the ground of non-possumus: 'I cannot say w'hat we will do, I have not any plans, i can only say that we have been considering it.' But it does not strike my right hon. friend that there is trouble in store for him there? Would it not have been the part of a cautious man, of a man who was husbanding the resources of this country, to have been very careful as to how he spent thirty-five million dollars of the people's money on that end of the road from Quebec down to the city of Moncton? What was the condition of things? You had a government road into which we had put $80,000,000 or $90,000,000 of the people's money; you had a road which was under almost annual deficits, due to lack of trade, or lack of management, and it would be clemency to my right hon. friend to say that it was due to lack of traffic. $80,000,000 or $90,000,000 of the peopl'es money invested in a road from Levis down to Moncton, St. John and Halifax. Would it not have been the part of caution to go very slow, not duplicating that road until a necessity had been shown therefor? But my hon. friend would not wait, would not be cautious, would not consider the matter at all, and the thing was carried through. Start it, build it, think about it, ponder Mr. FOSTER.
about it afterwards. Now what did my right hon. friend do? When it was objected that that ought not to be duplicated, he said: 'Distance is the essence of the matter, we will save from 120 to 140 miles from Levis to Moncton.' Did my hon. friend say that?-no doubt [DOT]about it. Did it go to the country with his impress?-no doubt about it. Did it help to elect him?-no doubt about it, in connection with other things. My right hon. friend had not even the reasonableness to take time enough to put a tape line over the country before he involved the country in an expense which is now amounting to $35,000,000. How does it come out after a tape line has been put on? What did you want to get? You wanted to get a four-tenths grade. The whole argument was-no good without a four-tenths grade. Will my right hon. friend be surprised if I tell him two things? First, that, as the road has been decided upon, he does not save 120 to 140 miles, but he saves only 29 miles. Will he take the other fact that if he had carried out his provision of having a four-tenths grade his road would have been two miles longer than the present Intercolonial Railway? How did he avoid the making it two miles longer? How did he save his 29 miles? He saved it by the device of murdering the grade. He has no road and never will have with a four-tenths grade, for the accomplishment of which he pledged his word and pledged the money of this people. An arithmetical calculation will have to take place. You have saved 29 miles, you have sacrificed your grade, you have to have two pusher grades of 10 and 12 miles and you have the permanent and perpetual cost of the operation of the pusher grades. Just the mere precaution of laying the tape over the ground would have told my hon. friend that he could not have saved 140 miles. But, he refused to wait for that. Now, what have we?- just what I have stated. I will put a question which was put before and to which we have had no reply. Would it not have been wise, when my right hon. friend saw the immense expenditure which was being put upon this country, to have gone slow upon that Quebec and Moncton end? Has he gone slow? When the Quebec bridge fell and he knew that it would be five, six or seven years before it could be built and of no use to him or to the road, would it not have been reasonable then to have gone slow? But my right hon. friend did not go slow. Up to this date he has spent $28,000,000 on that end. He told this House that it would not cost more than $10,000,000; yet, when it is finished, it will cost $35,000,000. In a year's time my right hon. friend, who is constructing a monu-

ment for himself, will have a disconnected end of a road through a locality which will give little or no local traffic, and a road which will compete with and starve to the extent that it gets traffic the government railway, into which we have put $80,000,000, and he will have it there at a cost of $35,000,000 more of this people's money. What will he do with it? Well, there are different kinds of monuments, but that is a kind of monument that I would not like to have pressing down on my remains. At the end of next year it will be built. Does my right hon. friend propose to put rolling stock upon it? That will be another great expense to the country. Does he propose to run it and have another parallel -Intercolonial railway with another parallel and still greater deficit in proportion to its length? So then we will have this delightful alternative, either to let it remain there silent, useless and depreciating or to work it at a loss, find the rolling stock, make all the expenditure and add again by deficits to the burden of the country. That is the simple alternative. Why, a man of business instinct and of business methods would have stopped that great expense even although a few millions had been spent, until the road had been brought within the reach and purview of practical operation. However, there my right hon. friend is. Just a little while ago a deputation waited upon him asking for aid for the Georgian Bay canal. Other deputations have asked for great public improvements which would have done good to the country. That section of territory had the Intercolonial Railway through it. My right hon. friend is only saving 29 miles and that at the expense of two costly pusher grades. He has taken $35,000,000 of the people's money, tied it up there forever, and he has to turn the cold face and the cold hand to propositions for the real and active development of this country in useful ways. There it stands. What is my right hon. friend going to do about it? How much better would it have been if he had taken a few millions of money and made the Intercolonial Railway just as good a road for freight hauling as he is making that new road from Levis down to Moncton. Why was not that done? That was our road, we had $90,000,000 or $100,000,000 in it, it was a burden upon us and a source of deficits, and it was that because of the lack of traffic and the difficulty of transport over it. Why would it not have been the part of prudence to have made it for all time to come a road, in grades and curves, which would compare with any Canadian railway and so utilize it, feed it and fatten it by the product of the west, which would be trained over the 500, 600,
or 700 miles of our own road? Why would not that have been the part of prudence? But instead of that my right hon. friend has got what he has got. Now, I must hurry on, but I want to call the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) to an argument that the Minister of Railways and Canals made and which was incidentally made by my right hon. friend as well. The Minister of Railways and Canals says that the paramount thing is to get the products out from the west. The Minister of Railways and Canals made a fine and flowery argument just about as near to the point as Timbuctoo is to the capital of this country. He said: 'Look at the homesteads which have been taken up in the Northwest; 13,000-15,000 homesteads have been taken up. Look at the people who are going into the Northwest; look at the grain that they will be raising for the sometimes starving peoples of the world in keeping with the advancing rate of wheat bread consumption.' It did not occur-or did it?-to my genial friend the Minister of Railways and Canals to inquire if there would have been one single homestead less taken up in the territory traversed by the Grand Trunk Pacific if never a dollar had been expended upon the eastern extension from Superior down to Moncton, which has involved us in $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 or $50,000,000 of absolute expenditure. Has a single homesteader gone in there because the country is spending $35,000,000 to parallel the Intercolonial Railway in the provinces of Quebec and New Brunswick? Not a single one. Will a single bushel of wheat be raised other than is raised now by the fact that we are building that road there at enormous expense? It all comes back to the fatal error, the error was this, that when a business man put before the Prime Minister a business proposition, the political instinct got the better of the business instinct and a political rather than a business railway was built.
A few million dollars in cash, maybe only a few million dollars of guarantee, would have built every mile of that line from the Great Lakes through to Winnipeg and through to the Pacific ocean, would have built every mile of it and we would have had everything that we have to-day with reference to the development of the west and the carriage of freight. This vast burden of $150,000,000 or more which was then assumed lightly and without forethought, to-day weighs upon us and burdens us, with no benefit commensurate with the expense. These northern regions of Ontario and Quebec might have been opened up but they might have been opened up later and gradually, and to the great benefit of Canada. For what

happpens to-day? To-day the Prime Minister has put clogs on the free feet of this Dominion-and heavy clogs they are. The Prime Minister went into this with a statement that $13,000,000 would build the road and yet before it is completed he will have added $180,000,000 to the	debt of this country, he will
strain the credit of this country, he puts himself and the country into this position that in order to carry out such a wild goose scheme he is sealing up the coffers, paralyzing the power of the Dominion of Canada to go on in other and useful ways of development. For many years to come there will knock at the gates of the Cabinet propositions which would be of the utmost benefit to us, demanding aid, and the Prime Minister's answer will have to be:	'Impossible. We have incurred such
an enormous expenditure with reference to this eastern section that we cannot aid you, we cannot aid you.'
Suppose that the alternative had been something like this: Take a few millions and make your Intercolonial Railway a good road. Take a few millions more if you like and subsidize the Grand Trunk Pacific from the lakes to the Pacific ocean -guarantees would have done it, there is not a foot of soil after that road leaves Winnipeg until it reaches almost the Rocky Mountains, there is not a mile of country which it passes through that will not, the moment it is opened, give the road its paying commerce. Hon. members talk about this loan being on all fours with the loan to the Canadian Pacific Railway. Why, you have put this line right in between two great lines of communication from Winnipeg west. The road is built through a country which in the main would have been served and served well by existing lines. But the point I wish to make now is that you put it through a country which was rich and which would offer traffic the moment that the transport was ready for it. A few millions of dollars would have done both of these things, a scratch of the pen on Mr. Hays' proposition to you would have put the traffic, when it came out of the Northwest, at the disposal of your Intercolonial Railway. Is there any doubt about that? There is Mr. Hays' proposition, there is what the Grand Trunk was willing to do, and to pledge itself to. That is what the hon. gentleman refused to have done. By adopting that plan you would have had the traffic secured, a line secured from the waters of the Great Lakes out to the Pacific and you would have it secured with very little pressure upon this country financially. Then if the Georgian Bay canal is a great economic and national undertaking, which would redound to the great benefit of this country in opening up deep water carriage Mr. FOSTER.
from the west down to the sea, if that is admitted, and if $100,000,000 would have built that canal, put that amount on one side. Then there is a demand that the Welland canal shall be deepened to a proper depth so as to accommodate the commerce on these lower lakes. That would cost somewhere about $40,000,000 and the two $140,000,000 against $180,000,000 or $200,000,000 that the government have bound around the neck of this country and for what outside of the great western branch of that line? You would have been able to contemplate that great line of internal canal transportation by the Georgian Bay canal and the southern line by the Welland canal, and you would still have been $40,000,000 better off than you are with neither of them completed, and with this burden of the eastern section upon the shoulders of this country. Can any one doubt as to which would inure most to the development and the benefit of Canada. The cheapening of the transport of the products of the great west, in this time of world-wide competition, which makes a cent a bushel almost the consideration which shall impel trade and which shall make the profits for the people who produce the grain, is a probleih of the greatest national importance. But instead of that you have this useless burden.
Let me make clear before I sit down, one point. Let no man say that my argument is an argument against the building of this line into and through the great Northwest and to the Pacific ocean. That is a matter about which there was no difference of opinion. It was the political ends that were tacked on to the project that we have objected to. They entailed great expense and were ahead of their time, they were not productive and will not be productive. What local products, from Moncton up to Quebec, will feed a railway? What local products from Quebec up to Lake Superior Junction will feed a great railway which in its maintenance and operation will be the most costly of any of the great railways of the Dominion? All that has been gained in the opening up of the great Northwest, in providing means of transportation and increased markets for Canadian products, would have gained by the alternative project of which I have spoken. Later on these adjuncts might have been built, but the country will ponder, more and more as the years pass on, the question whether it was necessary that, this costly addition, this costly duplication, should have been made at this time. One word more and it is this. If my hon. friend had not the privilege of being a member of this House and were carrying on this enterprise outside, if he were simply the promoter of a great company to build this road, and if, in his prospectus, he had stated the alleged facts that he has put

forth with reference to this great national undertaking, and had signed his name to that prospectus as he signed his name and gave his imprimatur to the public measure before the House, and had induced people to invest their money to the tune of $200,000,000, he would have found himself in the clutches of the law for issuing a prospectus entirely falsified by the facts. There are some advantages in being a member of parliament and, my right hon. friend will never have occasion to cease thanking his stars that he launched that scheme under the shelter of the privileges of parliament instead of outside parliament as a director and promoter.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The course taken by my hon. friends opposite is not at all a cause of surprise to me, nor, do I believe, to any body else. It is in keeping with their attitude from the first towards the great work in which we are now engaged. That attitude has been one of hostility and blind hostility, and it is manifest that the results of two elections have not yet opened the eyes of these hon. gentlemen. When in 1903 we brought into this House a Bill for the construction of another transcontinental railway, the object of which was to connect the waters of the Atlantic and the Pacific, every inch of which would be on Canadian ground, we were met from the other side with a storm of objections - objections to the terms granted, objections to the route selected, objections to the expenditure, objections to everything. They objected to the spirit and the letter of the Bill, to every line and every word of it, from the first to the last syllable. These objections were urged on this House, but they failed to make any impression. We were then told, however, that if we only dissolved the House and consulted the people, our project would be torn to pieces by an indignant electorate. When that legislation was completed in 1904, we thought that, in a project of this magnitude, it was due to the country that we should, before entry upon it, ask the opinion of the people. We dissolved parliament and then we had the question fought over again on the hustings as it had been on the floor of this House. All the arguments which had been urged in parliament against the project were urged on the hustings and with no greater success than before parliament. All the objections were thrust aside, and the public answer came clear, decisive and emphatic: go on with the work. With this high sanction, we started the enterprise; but as the work progressed, we found that we would have to revise our estimates. We found that our calculations had been too low and that the obstacles were greater even than we anticipated. The matter came up more 174
than once in the House. It has been thi3 session the subject of more than one debate, and my hon. friend, the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) frankly admitted that the cost would be much greater than we expected. Again we dissolved parliament and went before the people. Again the subject was discussed. Again all the new calculations were made before the public; and with all these facts before them, the electors gave the emphatic, decided answer:	go on and finish the work.
We thus have a double verdict. That verdict, twice given, ought to convince my hon. friends opposite that the people believe as we do and as we asserted in 1903, that this road is a political and a commercial necessity. And my hon. friend who has just spoken (Mr. Foster), and who has put the case in as false a colour as he could, has not been able to say that our scheme was ill conceived, that it is not a good commercial enterprise. All he could say was that it was premature, that there was no immediate necessity for the line from Moncton to Quebec or from Quebec to Winnipeg. He did not say that it should not be built. On the contrary, if his argument amounted to anything, he said that it must be built. And in concluding his remarks he said: 'Let me be understood as not hostile to the enterprise; all I say is that it came too early; we might have put our money into building railways more likely to pay dividends and later on build the line from Quebec to Winnipeg.' His whole argument was to that effect. If we had come, he said, to the House with a scheme for a continuation of the Grand Trunk Railway system from North Bay across the prairies to the foot of the Rockies, or across the Rockies to the Pacific ocean, the opposition would have gladly supported it. Well. I have only this to observe, that this mongrel idea of his was not the spontaneous inspiration of the moment. It came at a time when the opposition realized how deeply our scheme had gone into the minds and hearts of the people, and my hon. friends had to suggest something to save their faces. It was not the spontaneous act of the moment, but whether it came late or early, we would not accept the proposition. The proposition was made by the Grand Trunk Railway that we should favour a scheme to extend their railway from North Bay to the Pacific ocean. But we were opposed to that idea. Must I point out that the Grand Trunk Railway was built some 60 years ago, and built, not with regard to the future, but simply the needs of the moment. If we had adopted that suggestion, we would have had, not a national railway, but a hybrid railway, half Canadian and half American. The Grand Trunk Railway was built some 60 years ago simply for the needs of the day without any



thought of the morrow, and we are told that we should be as blind to-day as they were 60 years ago and commit the same grave errors. If that be the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite, it is not ours. Our policy is to have a national railway all through Canadian territory from the Atlantic to the Pacific. That was the idea we put before the people, and that is a policy which should appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite. Our policy is to bind the east and the west - the east, which was the cradle of the nation, and the west, which is now the hope of the nation-by means of that tie which commercial relations always create. Hon. gentlemen opposite do not favour that policy. Why? Because, in their opinion, a part of the route to be traversed by this road is not as good land as the prairies, because a part is barren, uninviting, unfit for settlement and incapable of maintaining a population. But, even if it were, would that be an argument against the scheme? In that case you never would have a national railway crossing the continent because the continent is not all fertile prairie. There are mountains, morasses and swamps, but the national idea is to have a Canadian railway from one ocean to the other. At 811 events that is our policy.
At one o'clock the House took recess.
House resumed at three o'clock.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I may be pardoned if I repeat the last thought to which I gave utterance before the recess, to the effect that the argument put forward by the opposition against the building of the Transcontinental Railway is no argument whatever. I stated that if it were an argument we never should have built a transcontinental railway; if it were a valid argument it was a mistake to build the Canadian Pacific Railway, since the section of that railway around Lake Superior runs for hundreds of miles upon a bed of granite rock upon which, as every body knows, there is not soil enough for grain to germinate or for trees to obtain firm root. If this were an argument we would have to consent submissively and impotently to take a position subordinate to and dependent on a foreign country. In the face of all this, I repeat that the policy which we adopted six years ago for the building of a transcontinental railway, is a commercial and a national necessity and if it suits the convenience of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House to contest and deny this proposition they are welcome to do so, and the more they deny it the more welcome they are to it. Is it true, as a matter of fact, that the whole section of country between the valley of the St. Lawrence and the prairies of the west, is, as has been represented,

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
predict, and never in election time, that the day is not far distant when the skeptics whom I see before me will also have to acknowledge the error of tneir way; but I am not certain whether they will do so or not.
But, Sir, even since we have started this project the events which have taken place amply justify the policy which we introduced nearly six years ago. Since 1903, when we introduced the grand project of building a transcontinental railway which should pass north of the Laurentian mountains, there has been, in those very mountains at Gowganda and at Cobalt, a discovery of minerals the like of which has never been found perhaps in any other part of the world. We have been accustomed to hear of the wonderful silver mines of Mexico, of Colorado, of Nevada, but what are they compared with the silver mines of Cobalt and Gowganda? And is it to be supposed that nature has exhausted her efforts in Gowganda and Cobalt? Is it to be supposed that she has not in her womb other Gowgandas and other Cobalts. Why Sir, the geological formation in which Gowganda and Cobalt are situated extends for hundreds of miles in all directions, and it is certain that we shall find other similarly rich districts. Already you have railways built or contemplated to reach those mineral claims, already you have railways running south and north to reach those valuable deposits. Suppose we had no transcontinental railway, those 'mines would have no permanence, they would have no outlet; but now they will be connected by railway communication with the Grand Trunk Pacific which runs east and northeast, and the cycle will be completed.
All these remarks apply in a like manner to other sections of the road, the section between the St. Lawrence and the maritime provinces, or to put it in exact words, the section between Quebec and Moncton. This is the section that has been made the special point of attack as absolutely useless, as a waste of money. I confess to some disappointment in the abbreviation of the distance over the existing railway; it is not as large as I had expected, it is not as large as I had believed. Looking over the map, which my hon. friend referred to this morning, I confess to some disappointment in that direction. Although the abbreviation is not as large as we had expected, still there is no reason to regret our enterprise. It is beyond doubt that the section of country which is to be covered by this railway is of the same character as the section of country which I have described. It is not all good, but there is in it some very valuable land. All this section which is in the counties of Levis, Dorchester, Bellechasse, Mont-magny, L'Islet and part of Kamouraska,

is a character equally as good as the best part of the eastern townships. It has the same formation, it has the same range of mountains, the Ailleghanies, which traverse the eastern townships; and what you have to-day in the eastern townships you will have in that section of the country, that is to say, fruit, dairy and cereal products, and valuable timber, everything which an agricultural community requires. In the counties of Kamouraska and Temis-couata, I understand, the country is rougher. In New Brunswick the country is fairly good. I cannot do better at this point than to give you the testimony of the engineer, which the chairman of the Transcontinental Railway Commission has kindly furnished me at my request. Mr. Foss, one of the engineers, writes as follows:
Report of the nature of the country and soil through that part of New Brunswick traversed by the Transcontinental Railway.
Generally the soil is fairly good and the country well fitted for agriculture.
From Moncton to Chipman, mile 0 to 59, about 10 miles, is through a cultivated region, and the balance is fairly well wooded, with a mixed growth of soft and hard wood, soil for the most part fairly good. From Chipman to the crossing of the Canada Eastern Branch of the Intercolonial Railway, mile 57 to 97, about 10 miles, through (a cultivated country, the balance fairly well wooded with a mixed growth of soft and hard wood, soil for the most part fairly good.
From the Canada Eastern Railway to the Tobique, mile 97 to 165, through a heavily wooded country, with soft wood in the low lands and heavy hard wood on the ridges. These ridges are good farming land, and the hard wood of value as soon as the railway is built. From the Tobique to Grand Falls, mile 165 to 197, about 12 miles, through farming lands or skirting along the edges of farms, the balance through heavy timber and land of mixed growth, the most of it excellent farming and grazing land.
From Grand Falls to the boundary of Quebec, mile 197 to 266, mostly in the St. John river valley, through a well settled country, with good soil.
This report is based on the personal knowledge of the writer, who has travelled over nearly every foot of the line in New Brunswick.
Very respectfully submitted,
(Signed) C. O. FOSS, District Engineer, District A.
This is as satisfactory as it can be. This is not, however, the reason why we built that section of the line, it was not for the development of that section that we built it. We built it rather for commercial and national reasons, because we believed, as I said, that this transcontinental railway, to be effective, must extend from one Canadian

water to the other Canadian water. I gave seme of these reasons when I introduced this project in 1903, and one of the reasons which I gave at that time was that we wanted to become absolutely independent of the bonding privilege, which at the present time makes us dependent upon the United States. This reason then put forward by myself has been strongly attacked; it was attacked this morning by the hon. member for. North Toronto, it was attacked the other day by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, who no doubt thought he had demolished my statement, at least to his satisfaction. In order to do him no injustice I will quote the very language which he made use of. I will give it just as it is in all its pointedness:
Six years have passed, and in the interim, as the right hon. gentleman well knows, we have not heard the slightest whisper or word about the repeal of the bonding privilege, and so it is that two-thirds of the speech which the right hon. gentleman then made before this parliament in reference to this matter stands as mere idle wind, designed as an excuse for undertaking this enterprise with such haste and such want of consideration.	_
It is very true that during the past six years there has been nothing to mar our good relations with the United States, but, is that a reason why we should not guard against the danger always existing, even although it is not always imminent? I might go much farther than the language of my hon. friend. It is very true that we have not had any trouble with our neighbours m the last six years. It is even truer, and I am glad of it, that our relations never were more cordial or more friendly than they have been in the last six years. It is also true, and I am proud of it, that since we have been in office we have had no difficulty with our neighbours. We have had sometimes small bickerings, which will occur occasionally in the best^ families, but we have had no serious conflict. We have had no serious quarrel with any one, and yet we are spending every year millions of dollars to defend our territory against a possible invasion. We spent $6,000,000 last year, and we have been spending $6,000,000 a year for some years past. I never heard this policy challenged by anybody. If 1 may refer to a past debate for a moment I might remind the House that ^ -my hon. friend from Nanaimo (Mr. Smith) spoke against the frills and feathers but, as to the substance of the expenditure no one nas ever ventured to cTititcise it. More than this, the hon. member for North Toronto, who', this morning, repeated this argument, introduced a motion into this House in order to induce us-to compel us-if possible, not only to provide for our defence on land but for our defence on sea as well. I agree with him that it is part of the duty of the nation to provide for its defence both by
land and on sea. But, is it any less a duty that we should secure our commercial independence against any possible interference with it? That is the motive which has impelled this course, and if my hon. friend takes issue with me upon this question, all I can say is so much the worse for my hon. friend.	...
Then, another reason why my hon. friend challenged our action in this respect was, that, in his estimation-at all events this was the statement which was made by him, this was the position which was taken by him and his friends when we introduced this project, the line which we are building between Moncton and Quebec will be absolutely barren of results, that it will be absolutely useless, that when the trade from the west had reached Quebec it would be as near Portland as it would be St. John. This sentiment was also shared by my gallant friend from Victoria and Haliburton (Mr. Hughes). I would have expected that sentiment from anybody else but himself, but I am sure that I was shocked and scandalized when I beheld the hon. member for Victoria and Haliburton taking such an unpatriotic attitude. I would have hoped that he would have stood by Canada and that he would have insisted that Canada should have an independent line to the sea.
