Will the right hon. gentleman be good enough to show where, either directly or indirectly, I have ever failed to stand by Canada? I have never gone to Washington and been kicked out.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I will show why, I think, the hon. member put the question he did a moment ago.
I was admiring the attitude of the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
But, it has been stated that this line would be of no avail because the Grand Trunk would turn away the trade from Quebec towards Portland. The Grand Trunk Railway Company, like everybody else, is animated by interest, and if we make it to the interest of the Grand Trunk, if we have a better railway than it can have from Quebec to Portland, I am sure that it will not prefer the inferior road. It is true that the railway does not come up to the standard that we had expected, but we are building from Quebec to Moncton a Tailway which generally will have a 4-10ths of one per cent grade. There is a pusher grade one way and a pusher grade the other way, but a train would be able to ascend the ridge with the help of one more engine-that is all- it is only for a short distance. So, on the the whole, we have a better road. But, is that the only way we can force trade through our own territory? We have already taken measures to have trade pushed in our own territory. Two years ago this House pass

ed a resolution unanimously, with the concurrence of the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden), with the concurrence of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and the concurrence of everybody who had a seat in this House, to this effect:
That on and after a date to be mentioned by the Governor in Council the British preference shall apply only to goods brought into Canada if shipped through a Canadian port.
That is a measure we have taken to compel trade to come to our own ports. Parliament has not exhausted its powers in this respect, and all I have to say upon this point is that the question of confederation has not been dealt with on geographical lines. It has been dealt with in a manner to give effect to the national idea, the political idea, the idea being to found upon this zone of the American continent a new nation endowed with British institutions, and everything that stands in the way of a realization of that idea must be overcome. That is the policy' of this government.
Another objection which I did not hear today but which I heard some few years ago from my hon. friend the leader of the opposition was that we did not make use of the Intercolonial Eailway. Yes, I also heard it from my hon. friend from North Toronto to-day, He asked:	Why did you
not make use of the Intercolonial Railway in order to extend the Transcontinental Railway to the maritime provinces? Why did we not make use of the Intercolonial Railway? For the same reason that the Conservative government of that day refused to make use of the Intercolonial Railway to extend the Canadian Pacific Railway to the maritime provinces? It is a matter of history as well that when the Canadian Pacific Railway had been extended from Callandar to Ottawa, from Ottawa to Montreal and from Montreal to Quebec, great pressure was brought to bear upon the government of that day to have the new National Railway extended from Quebec to the maritime provinces. The pressure was strong upon the government of the day and a legitimate pressure it was. They had to give way to it but did they take advantage of the Intercolonial Railway to carry out this extension of the National Railway to the waters of the Atlantic in Canadian territory? No, instead of that they subsidized a new line from Montreal to a maritime province port and subsidized it through the state of Maine. Why did they do that? Because it was found that the Intercolonial Railway was unsuited to the purpose of the Canadian Pacific Railway. What existed then exists to-day, and what was a good condition for the Canadian Pacific Railway is an equally good consideration for the Grand Trunk Pacific. Now, Sir, this is the Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
justification , of our policy, and I believe it is a sufficient and reasonable answer to all the objections which have been raised under this head.
A new objection is now brought to our attention. We are told: 'You are giving a favour to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, you are modifying the contract which you entered into with them in 1903 and 1004, and therefore it is legitimate that you should ask a price, that you should ask a compensation from the company for what you are giving to them. I have to repeat here what I stated a few days ago: that by this loan which we contemplate granting, we have made no modification whatever of the contract. We have not in any way modified the terms which were granted to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company in 1903 and 1904. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition stated that it was not a formal but it was a practical modification of the contract, and my hon. friend from Sim-coe (Mr. Lennox) went further-he never does anything by halves-and he stated it was not only a modification of the contract but a repudiation of the contract.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend adheres to his opinion?
That is what I say.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, if the idea which my hon. friend has in his mind, but which he has not given utterance to be correct; and if this be a clear gift to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, then my hon. friend is right that this would be a modification or a repudiation of the contract. But if it be not a gift but a loan; if the money is repaid, as I feel sure it will be repaid, what modification or repudiation of the contract will there be? I know my hon. friend's argument; he has stated that there is a repudiation, of the contract because the Grand Trunk Pacific Company has not undertaken to provide for the building of the railway out of their stock. He says they have $25,000,000 worth of stock, that they do not use that stock for the carrying out of the enterprise and that therefore it is a repudiation of the contract. But, as I said in 1903 I say now: time will not wait; we must go on with the enterprise. Does my hon. friend believe that in the present state of the money market the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company would be able to raise a great deal of money upon that $25,000,000 of stock? Does he believe that if they were to put it on the market now they would be able to raise sufficient capital to carry on the enterprise? Why, the hon. gentleman knows that at the resent time the stock would possibly not e saleable, and therefore the company has to wait until the market has sufficiently appreciated to make it to its interest and

to the interest of the country to realize upon it. Under such circumstances, and in view of the existing financial crisis the only manner in which the company could carry on the enterprise upon fair terms was to do what was done by the Canadian Pacific Railway in 1884 and come to the government and ask for the credit of the country to Taise the necessary money. My hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) stated this morning that this operation was not on all fours with the operation in 1884. What is the difference, let me ask him? In 188*1 the Canadian Pacific Railway Company found themselves in exactly the same position that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company find themselves in to-day. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company could not raise the money on the market and it therefore had to come to the government and co ask the credit of the government to carry on their project. I was struck with the argument used the other day by my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middlebro), and I shall refer to that argument now. By way of showing how much better were the terms that the government in 1884 made with the Canadian Pacific Railway than the government of to-day is making with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, he went on to give the value of the securities which were placed in the hands of the government at that time by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and he used these words:
In the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway contract, we had a first mortgage on 3,393 miles of railway, at, $50,000 a mile equal to $170,000,000; we had 21,000,000 acres of land, at $1.50 an acre, $31,500,000, a total of $201,500,000. Against that there was only a mortgage in respect of the Canada Central and other branch lines of $5,333,000; and land bonds outstanding to the net amount of $1,123,000; making a total enoumbrance of $6,456,000. Deducting this from the total value of the security received, leaves $195,044,000 of clear absolute security for the loan of $30,000,000. In addition to that, we had a first lien on the company's postal subsidies, on their steamships, on their after-acquired land, on the branch lines that they might thereafter build, and Dominion, provincial, or municipal subsidies, and upon all the property that they owned. So I think I am safe in saying that we had a security valued at $200,000,000 on which wt proposed to lend $30,000,000.
I have not a word to say against that statement; I have not the slightest exception to take to what the hon. gentleman says there; I believe that the securities which were offered to the Canadian government at that time are fully worth $200,000,000 today. But what were the conditions that faced the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in 1884? It was a young company composed of able and active men, and yet it was offering $200,000,000 in securities in order to borrow $30,000,000, and notwithstanding that company sought in vain to borrow one dollar from all the financial institutions of the world. It is a matter of history that in Montreal they exhausted their credit, that they went to New York without avail, that they went to the money markets of London and Amsterdam without success, and that having exhausted all their efforts they had to come to the government of Canada, and Canada had to lend them its credit to extricate them from the difficulty in which they found themselves. Is it extraordinarv, therefore, that if in 1884 the Canadian ' Pacific Railway Company could not raise $30,000,000 upon securities valued at six times that amount, that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company should to-day find it better financing and better business to come to the government and ask the credit of the govenment rather than to put their securities on the market at a very substantial loss. It seems to me that this is an argument which will appeal to the fairness and the common sense, even of my hon. friend from North Grey, and I feel sure he will apologize to the House for the very bad argument he made upon one point, even though he made a good argument on another point. It is true that we have not from the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company the same amount of securities that the government obtained from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Well, if we had been as generous to the Grand Trunk Pacific as the government of that day was to the Canadian Pacific Railway we might also have lots of securities to take as a pledge. If we had given to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company 25,000,000 acres of land; if we had given to the Grand Trunk Pacific some hundreds of miles of railway already built; if we had built for them the mountain section and the section along the north shore of Lake Superior, then we could have had from the Grand Trunk Pacific Company far better security than they are able to give us to-day. But, nevertheless, though they cannot give us their own security they give us an endorser in the person of the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada, which I think is quite solvent and quite able to answer for the amount which we are going to loan. I have heard this matter discussed; I know that there are skeptics on the other side of the House-I stated a moment ago that bad as it is, skepticism is the least of all the faults of hon. gentlemen opposite. For instance, my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) is satisfied that this loan will never be repaid, although it is guaranteed by both the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Railway Company itself. Does my hon. friend believe for one moment that the Grand Trunk Railway Company will make default on these bonds? They will be honoured, every cent of them.

I did not assert in any shape or by any inference that this loan would never be repaid; but if my right hon. friend asks me the question, I say, judging from the experience of the past, that there is great doubt whether it will ever be paid or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is exactly what I meant. I was sure my hon. friend would say that. I do not pretend to be a mind reader, but it is not difficult to read his mind. We know his way of thinking, and therefore the conclusion is not difficult to reach.
There is only one question as to which I think we can have reasonable discussion: it is as to the cost of the road. As to this there may also be some unreasonable criticism. The road is far more expensive than for my part I had calculated; but I will ask hon. gentlemen to name one of the great enterprises that go beyond the ordinary business of every day, in regard to which the estimates of the engineers have not been exceeded. It seems as if these gigantic enterprises, in the immensity and variety of their details, are never fully conceived in the minds of engineers, and almost invariably experience shows that there have been obstacles which were not thought of at their inception. The last century has been prolific in great enterprises, and I think I am safe in saying that it is not possible to single out one of them in which the estimate of the engineers has not been greatly exceeded. Perhaps the greatest work conceived during the last century was the digging of the Suez canal. The estimate of the engineers was that it would cost $20,000,000, and the canal was commenced in 1859 and was to be completed in 1864. It was not completed until 1869, and its cost turned out to be $80,000,000. In England one of the great works of the country was the building of the bridge over the Firth of Forth, which was built by two of the most eminent engineers of England, which of all countries is perhaps the most eminent in engineering science-I refer to Sir John Fowler and Sir Benjamin Baker. The estimate of the cost in our money was $6,400,000, and the cost of the work when completed exceeded $10,000,000. Coming to the United States, we find that the bridge over the East river between New York and Brooklyn cost 47i per cent more than the original estimate. If we come to Canada, the Victoria bridge is a monument of scientific engineering, a work of which we have reason to be proud, built by that eminent engineer, Robert Stevenson, and its cost was 35 per cent more than the original estimate. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition, in discussing this matter the other day, referred to the Panama canal; he also alluded to it a moment ago. It so happens that there is in the current Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
i	

issue of ' McClure's ' magazine an article on the Panama canal from the pen of no less a person than President Taft himself, who, as we know, had a good deal to do with that great work; and this is what he has to say as to its cost:
The second circumstance is with reference to the cost of the work. The estimate of the cost of the canal, exclusive of the interest during construction, sanitation, and expense of zone government, and the $50,000,000 paid Panama and the French Company, was $139,705,200. The present estimate of the cost of the canal as now projected, exclusive of the same items, is $297,766,000, or a grand total of $375,000,000.
So that the present estimate of the cost of the canal is over 100 per cent more than the original, and the canal is not built. When it is built, we shall know its real cost.
As I have said, the cost of the Transcontinental Railway has been in excess of what we had anticipated, but my hon. friend the Minister of Railways has given to the House what I think is the paramount reason for this. This road has been built upon a different plan altogether from the plan on which such roads are usually built. Railroads have usually been built first of all in as cheap a manner as possible-with heavy grades, inferior curves, wooden trestles and light rails; and afterwards the road is built and rebuilt. In this case the company has thought it better, and I believe it is wise economy on their part, instead of building a cheap road at first, to build at once a solid permanent road, instead of rebuilding the road three or four times over as the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has done. That is the reason the cost of the road has been greater tl an the estimate. I do not say this as an excuse, for whatever the cost of the road is, we must go on with the enterprise; but I am glad to say that there has been no extravagance, that every dollar of the money has been honestly expended. If we compare the cost of this road with the cost of similar enterprises, we find after all that the cost has not been excessive, but absolutely normal.
