I understand, however, that the cost of this railway, as finally adjusted, will not be $79,000 a mile, but about $60,000 a mile.
That includes watered stock, I presume.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have deducted the watered stock when I say that the cost will be $60,000 per mile instead of $79,000. Comparing the figures Dn our road with those, there is no reason why we should not be satisfied. These figures show that it compares very favourably with the standard railways.
Before I sit down, I wish to allude once and for all to the statement, which has been repeated for the thousandth time, that when I introduced this scheme I said all the road would cost would be $13,000,-
000.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There are men who assert in all seriousness that I said we were going to build a railway from the Atlantic to the Pacific, on the western section of which we were to contribute a guarantee for three-quarters of the cost, and build the eastern section from Winnipeg to Moncton, and that all this would be done for $13,000,000. My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) repeated that this morning without a blush or a smile. He was quite serious; well, if he did not deceive anybody, perhaps he deceived himself, and I am not sure of that either. I said in laying the project before the House that we were going to build the eastern section ourselves and lease it to the Grand Trunk Pacific for 3 per cent of the cost; we were going to assist in the western to the extent of three-quarters of the cost and for this also we were going to 'receive 3 per cent, but that on the two sections, we would give the company an abatement of interest for seven years, and that would represent the amount which would eventually come out of the Canadian people. Let me read the words once more to my hon. friends, not that I expect that they will change their tune, but to see if there be any sense of decency left in them:
When completed the company will lease the road and pay us a rental at the rate of 3 per cent per annum upon the cost of construction, whatever that may he. The same abatement of rent is provided also as in the case of interest on the western section. During seven years the company will be exempt from the payment of rent. For three years the company will be bound to pay the revenues and the tolls of the road if they amount to 3 per cent, and if they fail to amount to 3 per cent, then the difference between the revenues gathered and the 3 per cent will be capitalized and added to the cost of construction, and the company will pay interest upon it. So that here again the whole of the liability which is incurred by
the government for the building of that section from Moncton to Winnipeg is simply seven years of interest.
We had to advance the money but all the treasury would be mulcted for in the end would, be the seven years' interest, and I estimated that at $13,000,000.- 1 agree that this was a mistake because the road will cost much more; but to pretend that I said we would build the railway for $13,000,000 is something which would never come out of the brains of any one though it has come very often from the mouth of some. On this point, however, I claim no vindication. The facts are there, and I leave them once more with all confidence to the judgment of the Canadian people.
My hon. friend was kind enough to say that this railway would be a monument to my memory. I confess that I feel deeply upon it, I did my best to have the project accepted, not only by my colleagues but by parliament and the people, but I never heralded it as a monument to myself, though some people say I did. But I say the time will come when that policy will be vindicated to its fullest extent and to the very letter. The Canadian people little realize at this moment what is the future of this great enterprise. Is there a man, in or out of the House, who does not believe that it has a great future, or that it is not only a commercial but an absolute actual necessity.

Like every other hon. gentleman in this House, I have listened with a great deal of pleasure to the eloquent address delivered by the right hon. the Prime Minister. During his remarks he accused hon. gentlemen on this side of skepticism. I can only say that, having regard not only to the address we have just heard but to other statements made by the right hon. gentleman, I for one must plead guilty to the charge of being skeptical with regard to any statements made by him respecting this transaction. His charming language and fascinating manner would almost persuade one to become a skeptic, even if he were to rely upon that address alone. But this is not the first eloquent speech the right hon. gentleman has delivered on this question. He has delivered several on the question of the Transcontinental Railway and on many other subjects, and I do not propose to follow him through his somewhat lengthy utterances, but to touch merely on one or two points which he endeavoured to make at the opening of his remarks. One was that he was very anxious the products of this country should reach the sea-board wholly through Canadian territory. Let me congratulate the hon. gentleman upon his conversion to that doctrine. Only a few years ago he nailed the colours of unrestricted reciprocity to the ship of

state. At that time he was not only in favour of sending a portion of our products to the United States, but waxed eloquent in favour of sending all of them. I am very glad the right hon. gentleman has returned to the fold and recanted those opinions, *and congratulate him on having become a convert to the east and west lines of communication. But we always have some skepticism when listening to the eloquence of a new convert. We know that he is apt to be more enthusiastic than those who have borne the heat and burden of the day and are inclined to take what he said with more than a grain of salt. It is not surprising therefore that we should be a little skeptical.
The next position he took was that this transaction had on two or three different occasions received the endorsation, not only of this House, but of the country. Let me say that, in my humble opinion, neither the representatives of the people in this House nor the people themselves have had an opportunity of expressing an unprejudiced opinion on this scheme of the national transcontinental railway. What was the modus operandi? A contract was entered into at first with the Grand Trunk Pacific by the government, subject to the ratification of this House. The leader of the House came down here with a signed contract, and the question with his followers was whether they should support that contract and have the government remain in office or reject it and have the government resign from office. It was a question of confidence or non-confidence, and the followers of the government voted, not on the merits of the case, but in order that their party might remain in power. But, Mr. Speaker, when the matter first came before this House for ratification, did the right hon. gentleman present the facts, or anything within reasonable distance of the facts regarding this contract? I remember the eloquent speeches that he delivered in those days. We remember him telling the people of this country that we had mountains of information. At page 7680 of ' Hansard ' of 1903, he said.
In that year, 1872, the Canadian government undertook a systematic and scientific exploration of the whole northern region from Lake Abitibi westward to the Pacific ocean. Prom the year 1872 to the year 1880 no less than twenty-eight expeditions were organized to visit, explore, and report upon that country. . . . Mr. Marcus Smith, Mr. Cambie, Mr. Hunter, Mr. Gordon, Mr. Horetzky, and several others, all engineers of eminence, crossed and recrossed that territory and became as familiar with it as they were with the streets of Ottawa.
We are all proud of the Prime Minister, proud that we have a poet as Prime Minister, as is evident in this very sentence: Mr. CROTHERS.
'Crossed and recrossed that territory and became as familiar with it as they were with the streets of Ottawa.' And his followers behind him cheered him to the echo.
Any one who to-day would care to look into the reports now accumulated in the archives of the Railway Department will know that country, just as he may know his own home.
So the right hon. gentleman knew this country and he was speaking of that portion of the road. He spoke of the portion east of Lake Abitibi in the province of Quebec which he said had been explored several times. Now with all that information touching that road, knowing it as he knew his own home, or the streets of Ottawa, he told the people of Canada that this road would cost us only $13,000,000. That, of course, was not to be the total cost of constructing this road, but the sum that the people of Canada would have to pay by way of interest. I understood that at the time and I do not think the people of Canada were misled on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: Hear, hear.

The Prime Minister took the position that if the people of Canada were to borrow hundreds of millions to put into this road, they would only be required to pay that amount of interest. I am only surprised that with his eloquence, with his ingenuity, with his capacity, the Prime Minister did not go a little further and prove to the people of Canada not only that it would only cost $12,000,000 or $13,000,000, but that it would not cost them a cent to construct the road. Why? Because the minister proposed to go to England and borrow the money. He might have gone a step farther and have said to the people of Canada: 'It will not cost you a cent because at the end of each year, when the interest comes due, I will go to England and borrow the money. The Prime Minister based his statement that it would not cost the country more than $12,000,000 or $13,000,000 upon figures supplied to him by the Minister of Finance, who estimated that the eastern section of the road would cost $51,300,000. That estimate was arrived at after very close calculation on the part of that great financier, the Finance Minister of Canada. He knew then, as he knows now, that these great enterprises always cost two or tree times as much as the original estimate, but he made that statement and it was repeated by every one of his followers throughout the country. Yet the Prime Minister has the courage to announce in this House that he received the endorsation of the people of Canada. I do not wish to say anything offensive or to accuse the Prime Minister of intentionally making a statement that was not true or of intentional misrepresen-

tation, but I do say that when these statements were made to parliament and through parliament to the people, parliament and the people of Canada were both grossly misled. I am surprised at the courage of the Prime Minister, after admitting to-day that that section will cost at the least $150,000,000, in saying that in 1904 he received the approval of the people of Canada with regard to this measure.
Coming down to the election campaign of 1908, the right hon. gentleman visited the province of Ontario and he was apparently so busy there in satisfying the people of Ontario that he was a straight Grit, that he had no time to discuss the Grand Trunk Pacific. He said, as reported in the 'Globe':
I am a straight Grit. Not an independent Grit (cheers), but a Grit out and out, and the man who is nearest my heart is the man who is a Grit like myself and it is as a Grit that I ask you all, ladies and gentlemen, to give your support to my friend Mr. Smith.
Mr. Speaker, statesmanship, elegance, dignity and patriotism:	No appeal to intelligence, no appeal to the judgment of the people, no appeal to conscience, no appeal to patriotism, no argument in favour of constructing the Transcontinental Railroad, but: ' I am a straight Grit, not an independent Grit, but a Grit out and out.' The right hon. gentleman's experience satisfied him that this was the most effective style of argument. He might have said not only that he was a straight Grit, but that he was a fossilized Grit and that he appealed to fossilized Grits in the province of Ontario, not that he appealed to their judgment, to their conscience, or that he appealed to them on high national principles for their votes. Then he went down to the province of Quebec. Did he there tell anything about the cost of the Transcontinental Railway? Did he give such an eloquent description of what it will do for the country as he has done to-day? Did he appeal to the conscience, the independence, the patriotism of the people of Quebec? What was his appeal?
The same blood flows through my veins that flows through yours.
And, Mr. Speaker, when he came to Ottawa, he saw a report of a speech delivered by his colleague and the only thing that struck him in that speech was the opinion of his colleague touching the increase in the salaries of the Civil Service in Ottawa. He wrote a letter to his colleague saying: 'I quite endorse your opinion touching the increase of the salaries of the Civil Service, and you have my permission to say so.'
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister of Canada, the man standing at the head of the nation, the man whose office we all admire and respect and esteem and Tevere, might have been expected to have appealed to the people on a higher plane than that. We
would have expected the right hon. the Prime Minister of Canada, if his colleague in Ottawa had suggested to him the propriety of writing such a letter to the people of Ottawa, we would have expected him to say, 'No, Mr. McGiverin, I am not running this election on a peanut policy. I am at the head of the government of Canada. The interest of Canada, the great transactions in which we are engaged, are of more importance than your success or mine. I do not propose to discuss with you at this time such a small question as the salaries of the civil servants at Ottawa. There are great national questions at issue. My sentiments, my interest in the people of this country, my patriotism, force me to say to you that I will not descend to these insignificant questions.'
Now, Mr. Speaker, when we had that campaign in Quebec, when we had that campaign in Ontario, when we had that campaign in Ottawa, does it not require considerable courage on the part of the Prime Minister to stand up before us and boast of the people of Canada having on several occasions approved of what he has done in regard to the Transcontinental Railway? Now with these mountains of information, we had the right hon. gentleman telling U3 in eloquent terms-because he is always eloquent, we are always delighted to hear him, we are always proud of him. His charming language and his fascinating manner, as I said a moment ago, almost convert those who are sitting opposite to him-but with all this information, with the knowledge he then had of the diflerent parts of this country, equal to the knowledge he had of his own home, as familiar with these different sections as he is with the streets of Ottawa, he told the people of Canada that the eastern division would only cost $51,300,000. He has cited two ot three other cases here to-day where the actual cost was a great deal more than the first estimate. I think the largest difference he mentioned was 100 per cent. Now we have it admitted that this eastern division will cost $150,000,000. 50 in 150 goes three times. How much percentage is that? 300 per cent. I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that he is not able to find a parallel in the whole railway history, in all modern engineering, where the real cost so far exceeded the estimates. We were told also that we were going to save from 120 to 140 miles by the construction of this road through New Brunswick; and to-day it is admitted that we are saving about 29 miles. The right hon. gentleman was familiar, from the explorations, from the documents in the archives, as familiar with the whole road across to the Pacific as he was, he told us, with his own home, with the streets of Ottawa. The right hon. gentleman told us that the mountain sec-

tion was about 600 miles in length, and his colleague the Finance Minister put it at 480 miles. What have we now? It is now stated by the Finance Minister that the mountain section is 839 miles, and in a letter which Mr. Hays wrote to the Finance Minister on the 16th of November last, this prairie section has been extended 130 miles further west than it was contemplated at the time the agreement was made; 839 and 130 will give you 969 miles as the length of that mountain section at that time. And yet we have the right hon. gentleman putting it at 600 miles, with his mountains of information; and we had the Finance Minister putting it at 480 miles, with his mountains of information. So, Mr. Speaker, what is one of the most discouraging and humiliating features of this whole transaction, is the utter unreliability of the statements that are made by hon. gentlemen opposite, not only the unreliability with reference to the original statements they made buit the unreliability of, "the statemen(ts they have recently made. I do not see, Mr. Speaker, how hon. gentlemen in this House can vote on this question, and vote intelligently, how they can be otherwise than in the condition in which the right hon. gentleman describes us, that of skeptics. Why, no longer ago than the 13th day of April, 1908, just one year ago, the Minister of Railways brought down a return to this House stating that the prairie section would cost $21,873,000-only one year ago. What have we now? We have it stated now that the $11,000,000 we raised has all been expended except I think $1,000,000; the $10,000,000 raised by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company on guarantees given by the Grand Trunk Railway Company will make you over $20,000,000; the Grand Trunk is to get back $7,000,000 now of this sum we are advancing, and that makes up about $27,000,000, and there are about 600 miles of it constructed. When I saw this letter that was sent to the Finance Minister on the 16th day of November, I supposed in my innocence,- and I think the people supposed, that that $10,000,000 was asked for to enable the company to continue the construction of the prairie section on to the mountain section. I will read a sentence or two from that letter:
By reason of the extension of the prairie section 130 miles further west than was contemplated, it is found that an additional sum of $10,000,000 will be needed to complete the section to Wolf Creek which is the dividing line between the prairie and mountain sections. To raise this additional sum it will be necessary to make a further issue of bonds as contemplated by section 34 of the agreement of the 29th July,' 1903. . . . Further legislation will be required to enable the company to fully carry out what was contemplated by these agreements respecting the issue of bonds to provide the balance rerequired-

To provide the balance required.
-(above the proceeds of the government guarantee) for the completion of the prairie section of the western division, and we desire to have an assurance that your government will, at the forthcoming session of parliament, introduce and support such legislation at the earliest date practicable. . . . Under such circumstances and in view of the urgent desire of the government that the enterprise shall be prosecuted without any delay, we ask the government to assist us in the utilizing of these bonds.
And so on. Near the end of the letter he says, speaking of this sum required for the completion of the prairie section:
I would therefore urge that such measures of immediate relief he given as will enable us to do this and avoid the disastrous effect on the credit of both the railways and the country which would necessarily result from a stoppage of the work.
Now, Mr. Speaker, reading that letter any one would come to the conclusion that the work already done had been paid for, and that $10,000,000 was required to continue the construction work. I submit that that was a misleading statement to make, misleading to members of this House and misleading to the people of this country. We all understood at that time that the $10,000,000 was required to continue the work on to the mountains. And what are we told now? We are told that about $7,000,000 of the $10,000,000 is already expended, and that there will be only $3,000,000 left. Then, Mr. Speaker, it has been in substance admitted by the right hon. gentleman and by the Minister of Finance, that negotiations were afoot with the officers of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company prior to the 26th of October last. Why did not the right hon. gentleman and why did not the Finance Minister mention that in discussing these matters or in discussing any other matters with the people of Canada? Was the little sum of $10,000,000 too small and too insignificant for them to submit to the people of Canada? Why did they withhold it? Is it not in keeping with their whole conduct in regard to this matter? Does it not appear to have been the well settled policy that this government should humbug the people in reference to this Transcontinental Railway? The Minister of Finance was up in our province during the elections. These negotiations were going on with the president of the Grand Trunk Pacific, but he never uttered a sentence to the people of Ontario with respect to them. He was too busy telling the people of Ontario, why he had expended such large sums of money. He told them that he had expended these large sums of money because he had them to expend. The most reckless spendthrift in the country might say: ' I have spent all

I had because I had it to spend.' The prodigal son might have said: ' I have squandered the substance which my father gave me, in riotous living because I had it to spend.' But the time came when he fain would have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat, and no man gave unto him. Yet, in the face of this we find the right hon. gentleman coming to this House, and, through this House, saying to the people of Canada that they should approve of this loan of $10,000,000, that they have already approved of it two or three times, that his soul is so lofty that he is thinking only now of keeping our products out of the United States and that he has reformed since; a few years ago, he nailed the colours of unrestricted reciprocity to the mast and declared that he would never tear them down until they waved triumphant. As far as I am concerned I confess that I plead guilty to being a skeptic. I also submit that the conduct and the statements of these hon. gentlemen in 1903 and 1904, and often and often repeated since, would convert the firmest believer into the most pronounced skeptic.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Mr. Speaker before the Bill is read a third time I desire very briefly to present some considerations to the House in connection with the proposal. The right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has referred to the supposed skepticism of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House with regard to the resources of this country and he has repeated the parrot-like cry that has resounded throughout this country from one end of it to the other, whenever a Liberal orator ascended a Grit platform, that the Conservative party, in 1903 and 1904, opposed the project of the Transcontinental Railway. I take issue with the right hon. gentleman on that point as I take issue with him on some other points and I say that we declared then, as we declare now, that the Conservative party which carried to a triumphant issue the proposition to build a transcontinental railway across this continent in days gone by, have always shown that they had and have the courage, the faith and the belief in the resources of this country that should characterize every patriotic citizen of Canada. I was a little surprised at the audacity of the right hon. gentleman in reference to the skepticism of the Conservative party in regard t-o the resources of Canada. I think that it indicated that the right hon. gentleman's nervous system is increasing in force and vitality as the years go by.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs
speechtext: That is good.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman state the date of that report?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
1902. My right hon. friend has referred to the speech of my hon. friend from North Toronto and has said that he spoke of some hybrid scheme. As far as I can understand the only hybrid scheme to which he has alluded was the proposition of the Grand Trunk Pacific in the first instance. The Prime Minister said that that scheme was half Canadian and half American. What do you think of a scheme for a national transcontinental railway upon which this country has paid out, or will contribute in cash and credit, perhaps $225,000,000 or $250,000,000, and which has its winter port, as far as we can understand at the present time, in the United States of America and not within the limits of Canada at all, a point to which I will direct attention again and to which I will ask the consideration of the House by a resolution I shall move.	_
But my right hon. friend excelled himself when he came to deal with the bonding privilege. The chief consideration placed before the House by the right hon. gentleman in 1903 was the imminence of danger by reason of the possible or probable abrogation of the bonding privilege by the government of the United States. He admitted to-day that we have not heard much about the abrogation of the bonding privilege since he made that famous speech in 1903, but he still persists in asserting that Canada has been saved from some great impending danger by the course he took at that time. Let me ask the right hon. gentleman three questions. Did or did not the Intercolonial Railway exist before the 30th day of July, 1903? Is or is not the Intercolonial Railway built wholly upon Canadian territory? Does or does not the Intercolonial Railway connect at Montreal with the Canadian ' Pacific Railway system? These are three pertinent questions which I have the rght to put to the right hon. gentleman, and which touch the very essence of his argument that the $30,000,000 or $35,000,000 expended on the National Transcontinental Railway from Quebec to Moncton has been of any real service to Canada with respect to the bonding privilege. And, Sir, the net result of it all is that Canada has been saved from this tremendous danger in connection with the bonding prvilege by the construction of a railway line at an Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
expense of $30,000,000, which saves 29 miles of distance between Quebec and Moncton. It is thus that in the mind of the right hon. gentleman Canada has been saved from such dangers as he pointed out in 1903, and reaffirmed this afternoon. Can absurdity go farther? The Intercolonial Railway is upon Canadian territory. The Intercolonial Railway, according to the statement of the Minister of Railways this very session, desires and requires all the further traffic that can be placed upon it, but the right hon. gentleman persists in saying that we have been saved from some awful danger by the mere fact that we have shortened the line between Quebec and Moncton by 29 miles.
My right hon. friend further stated that in 1903, I declared that the line from Quebec to Moncton was absolutely absurd and useless. I did not make any such declaration. I did not then have sufficient information tc enable me to judge one way or the other, nor, as the results have shown, did the right hon. gentleman possess any such information at that time. What I said then and what I repeat now is :
As to my attitude with regard to the Que-bec-Moncton line, I say that if there is to be found a better and shorter line between Riviere du Loup, or any other point on the Intercolonial, and Moncton, a line which will give to Halifax and St. John, and the maritime provinces generally, a better fighting chance for western traffic than that which they have at present, I will support its construction. But I will not support it with the object for which this Bill provides. I will support the construction of that line a9 part of the Intercolonial Railway. I do not believe in constructing that better and shorter line for the purpose of handing it over to the Grand Trunk Pacific or any other railway company, but I do believe in constructing it and keeping it for the people's railway. That is my position, and it is a position which I am ready to discuss in the maritime provinces or anywhere else.
I went on to elaborate the argument, but I will not weary the House by quoting further. My right hon. friend also referred to a resolution passed by this House some sessions ago with respect to goods admitted to Canada, and claiming the British preference, but I would point out to him that if the statement of his own Minister of Railways is to be taken at its face value, and if the Intercolonial Railway requires all the traffic it can get, it is rather singular that the right hon. gentleman does not put that policy into force at once and give to the Intercolonial Railway a better chance of getting traffic than it enjoys to-day.
The right hon. gentleman told us that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company could not raise anything upon its stock ; but I would point but that if the Canadian Pacific Railway Company in 1882, in view of the denunciation of the scheme by the Liberal party of that day, at a time when that

western country was unknown, when the land was inaccessible, when the people of Canada and of the world at large had not that faith and confidence in it which they have to-day; if the Canadian Pacific Railway at that time could induce the promoters of the enterprise to take its stock at 25 cents on the dollar and afterwards at 50 cents on the dollar, it is to say the least peculiar that in these later days when that country has been populated to a very considerable extent, when immigration is pouring into it, when this enterprise is declared to be a paying enterprise from the very moment it commences to carry freight; it is I say a remarkable thing that the promoters of that enterprise 'have not put a dollar of their money into the road, but are depending absolutely upon bond issues, moneys raised by the guarantee of the government and of the Grand Trunk Railway Company.
Then the right hon. gentleman referred to the 250,000,000 acres of land granted by the government of Canada to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, but he very discreetly omitted to mention that the government of which he was a member offered a very much larger quantity of land for the purpose of constructing that railway and were not able to get it constructed.
Leaving the speech of my right hon. friend for a moment and coming to what I have more immediately in mind, I recognize, as I have already said, that this enterprise upon which so much money has been spent both in eastern and western Canada, must be carried to a conclusion, and that it would be a misfortune that any stoppage of the work should take place. But we have to consider the object of this enterprise, and that object is set forth in the agreement of 1903 as follows:
Whereas it is in the interest of Canada that a line of railway, designed to secure the most direct and economical interchange of traffic between eastern Canada and the provinces and territories west of the great lakes, to open up and develop the northern zone of the Dominion, to promote the internal and foreign trade of Canada, and to develop commerce through Canadian ports, should be constructed and operated as a common railway highway across the Dominion, from ocean to ocean, and wholly within Canadian territory.
I need not again allude to the fact that paragraphs 42 and 43 of this agreement declare specifically that aid was granted to the enterprise by the government of Canada for the express purpose of encouraging the development of Canadian trade and transportation of goods through Canadian channels to Canadian ports. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company was pledged to the fulfilment of that condition and to use its best efforts for the purpose of carrying it out. But, in the first place the method by which the government sought to accomplish this was by selecting a company
which had its chief winter port in the United States. That was an extraordinary feature of the whole enterprise. The object of this enormous public aid being that we should build up our own Canadian ports both in summer and winter, it does seem remarkable that a company was selected which has its winter ports altogether in the United States. I say that with no desire to cast any discredit upon the Grand Trunk Railway Company. It has its own commercial interests to serve; it has built up Portland, it has enormous interests there, it has expended enormous sums of money at that port, and I am not blaming the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company for endeavouring to make the best bargain it could with this government or with any one else with respect to its business enterprises. But the initial difficulty, a difficulty from which this government and this country can never get away, was that the company selected to assist the government in carrying out this enterprise was a company that had its winter port in the United States and not in Canada.
The next feature of the enterprise to which attention may be directed is that the undertaking was not to be carried out by means of a contract with the Grand Trunk Railway Company. If that company had been a party to this contract, it would have been forced by the voice of the Canadian people, as any government entering into such a contract would have been found to accept effective stipulations to use Can-dian ports during the winter months. But that was not done. It was the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company alone which entered into the stipulations in regard to the development of Canadian trade through Canadian channels.
Another feature was that the promoters were not required to put any money into the enterprise themselves, but were allowed to build it by bond issues-I am speaking of the western division-guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Railway Company and by the government, while the government undertook the entire financing of the construction of the eastern division. There has been an enormous drain upon the resources of our country for this work. Its purpose is to bring the enormously increasing traffic of the west to Canadian ports instead of leaving it to be diverted to ports in the United States; and yet what will be the inevitable result of the conditions which I have presented to the House?
My right hon. friend said he presented this enterprise to the people of this country with a firm heart. Does he present to-day with a firm heart the imminent danger that all that traffic will be carried in the winter to Portland instead of to St. John and Halifax? Is it for this purpose that the people of this country have supplied their cash and pledged their credit to the extent of $250,000,000? What was

my right hon. friend's answer when I put this question to him in the most pointed manner a few days ago? What was his answer when the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) put it to him to-day and asked him what he was going to do about it? His answer to me was that the clause should be carried; and his answer to the hon. member for West Toronto was a complete avoidance of the question. There will be a lease of the section from Winnipeg to the Port Arthur branch and western traffic will he delivered to the Grand Trunk Railway, which, under the conditions as they stand at present, will be at liberty during the winter months to carry it to Portland instead of to St. John or Halifax. My right hon. friend tells us that he will select a more favourable occasion-when the lease will be granted to this company of the line from Winnipeg to the Port Arthur branch-for dealing with this question. I have already pointed out that the terms of the lease are already settled-that any lease of a portion of the line must, so far as the company is concerned, be on terms not more onerous to them than those of the lease of the entire line. I have pointed out further that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company has the option of taking or not taking a lease of any portion of the line. Is there any answer to my argument that under these conditions the traffic is bound to go to Portland in the winter months? My right hon. friend says that the insertion of any necessary stipulation binding upon the Grand Trunk would be a modification of the contract. On that matter there may be a legitimate difference of opinon ; but I adhere to my view that although there has been no formal modification of the contract, there is by the proposal of the government a practical modification of the contract. But if I accept my right hon. friend's assurance in that regard, then he is open to this retort, that if his proposal is not a modification of the contract, no more would it be a modification of the contract to insist that the Grand Trunk Railway Company should bind itself by some effective stipulation. It is not a party to the contract, and therefore to insist that it shall enter into some stipulation of that kind would be, according to the reasoning of my right hon. friend, no modification of the contract, and there is no reason why it should not be done. Therefore it seems to me that this is a time for action by the government; and, as they do not seem disposed to take any action in behalf of the maritime ports of Canada, I propose to make a suggestion by the terms of a resolution which I shall offer. Mr. Blair in this House, in 1903, pointed out, and with good reason, that in days to come the expenditure, which he put at that time at Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
$15,000,000, now swollen to $30,000,000 or $35,000,000, would be taken into consideration as an expenditure for the transportation requirements of the maritime provinces in the future. But the feeling in the minds of the people of the maritime provinces will be that this expenditure should not be placed against them in the records of the country's expenditure when they find that this great national transcontinental highway will be utilized for carrying the trade of Canada to Portland instead of to the ports of the maritime provinces. That will be the net result, and is it a Tesult to which my right hon. friend looks forward with a firm heart? I do not believe that the people of the maritime provinces will _ look forward to it with a firm heart, or with a rejoicing heart, but I think they will be firm in heart against proposals which _ look to a continuance of any such condition. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move:
That the order for the third reading be discharged and that the said Bill be referred back to Committee of the Whole House with power to amend the same by adding effective provisions binding the Grand Trunk Railway Company as well as the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to fulfil the conditions upon which aid has been granted to this enterprise, namely, the development of trade through Canadian channels and Canadian ocean ports and forbidding the diversion of Canadian traffic to foreign ports except when specifically routed thereto by the shipper.

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to have taken any part in this debate, but some observations have been made by hon. gentlemen opposite which are quite contrary to my conception of this enterprise and to the advisability of making the loan under the circumstances which have been presented to the House. It has been argued that the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Canadian Northern offers as great security, from a military point of view, for connections between the west and the east as does the Grand Trunk Pacific. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) said that the Grand Trunk Pacific was not the most northerly road, that there were other lines extending farther north, and that consequently it was not as well located as regards military use or that it would be of as much advantage to the country in case of need as some of the existing lines. Well, while the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) is usually very logical and very well informed on any subject he discusses, I do not think he did himself justice in dealing with this matter, because I cannot but think that if he had made himself fully acquainted with the positions of the several lines of railway to which he referred, he would not have contended that there is

any comparison, from a military point of view, between the Canadian Pacific Railway and the National Transcontinental. What are the conditions? It was said, why, the Transcontinental starts at Halifax, at Quebec, at Winnipeg, and so on from point to point across the country. That is true, but it is also true that from Quebec to Winnipeg its line is much more northerly situated than the Canadian Pacific Railway, and also that in this section it is a trunk line of communication between the east and west. That is to say it is the heart of the connection between the east and the west, and cannot be left out of the calculations if you have any regard for maintaining connection between the east and the west, assuming that we might unfortunately be involved in a contest with our neighbours to the south. The conditions are these: The Canadian Pacific Railway skirts for 250 miles the north shore of Lake Superior. I am not posing here as a military expert by any means, but I know sufficiently of military tactics, and national defence, to make this assertion, that, as a means of maintaining communication between the west and the east, in the event of trouble, the Canadian Pacific Railway is almost valueless. With anything like a powerful enemy, that line would be almost impossible to defend. It could be attacked at a hundred points during any night at all, whether bright or dark, with certainly, so far as the attacking force might be concerned, and with uncertainty so far as regards the defence, so that, from a military point of view, it would be particularly vulnerable. The Canadian Northern is not yet constructed in that section. It will be further inland than the Canadian Pacific Railway, but, after all, if it follows the line already located, it will be within very easy striking distance of the lake shore, whereas the Transcontinental runs 200 miles north, and at no point much less than 150 rhiles north. In my opinion this government would be justified in spending every dollar that this line will cost, if for no other reason than that they will thereby make Canada more capable of defending her liberty and national rights in case of attack. But that is not the object altogether of building the road. The hon. gentleman from North Toronto (Mr. Poster) said that the railway started from Quebec. Let me submit that Quebec is a pretty safe point to start from. There is not a stronger fortification on the continent and therefore it mav be taken as a very good point to start from, regarded in the light of national defence. Then between Quebec and Winnipeg, when we consider the rugged character of the country and its local conditions, there is no nation on this globe that could dislodge the Can-175
adian people from that position if they chose to defend it.
There are other features of the debate in which I cannot agree. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) have pointed out on several occasions that, in their opinion, there is a weakness in the agreement because there is a connection from Fort William and Port Arthur by a branch line to a junction with the Transcontinental of some 200 miles, and they represented that traffic routed to Fort William, and delivered at the head of the lakes and by the Transcontinental, will be routed from there over the Grand Trunk Railway system to American ports. I cannot agree in that contention. When traffic reaches Port Arthur and Fort William, it is not necessarily the traffic of the Grand Trunk Pacific or the Grand Trunk Railway. It is everybody's traffic.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

It is the traffic of the common carriers of the country, and they will take part in it. The Canadian Pacific Railway does not carry through its own line, by any means, all the traffic it delivers at these ports today, and neither will the Grand Trunk Pacific after it is built. Let me contrast that position with the position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite. They say it would have been better had the Grand Trunk Railway been permitted to build from North Bay to the western prairie and thus carry out the scheme to which these hon. gentlemen say they are still wedded. But where would the traffic go then? If the Grand Trunk Pacific carried it over its trunk line, to its connection with the eastern system, at North Bay. we would not have as much power of preventing the routing of that traffic through American ports in the interests of their own line as we now -have in the case to which I have referred. There is the other alternative, that during the winter months freight may go, not to the head of the lake, but over the line to Montreal or Qeubec or other points in Canada through the Grand Trunk Railway system, and that therefore it may possibly be routed to American ports. I do not agree in that. There may be something in it, I do not say it is a thing to which we should shut our eyes by any means, but let me ask hon. gentlemen how they can contend that even in these circumstances it would be more likely to be carried through or routed to an American port than it would be if the connection was made at North Bay instead of at Quebec or Montreal. I cannot understand that logic, I do not think the conditions of traffic lend themselves to that argument by any means.



The prediction in regard to the eastern section of the line has been discussed on former occasions. Hon. gentlemen opposite predict that there will be a deficit, that the eastern section of the line will not pay. We have heard similar predictions on former occasions. I remember that when the Canadian Pacific Railway proposed to build a line from Toronto to Montreal, many people predicted that the road would be bankrupt, that it would never pay; but we have seen that it has paid, it is doing a good business to-day and it has not destroyed the Grand Trunk Railway. The contention was that to build a parallel line was unjust to the Grand Trunk and that both lines would be unremunerative to the shareholders and deter capital from coming to this country. I heard those arguments upon the political platform then, but those gloomy predictions have not been fulfilled. That^ line has done a good business from the time of its construction. The history of railway construction and of transportation is that these lines of railway not only beget traffic, but they create such prosperity, such development, such incre.ase in the product and in the ability to travel on the part of the people in the adjoining country, that the building of one line even paralleling another line, assists the line whch it parallels. Let me give a case in point. The best paying railway on this continent, or for that matter on the continent of Europe, is the line of railway that parallels the cheapest line of transportation, I refer to the New York Central, which, for 440 miles, parallels the Erie canal, practically from the shores of the great lakes to the city of New York. Why is it the best paying line? It is not a single track line, it has four tracts and is doing the greatest business in relation to its mileage of any road in the world. It competes with the Erie canal, which is the cheapest means of transportation to the ocean port of New York. The people in its vicinity are able to make more money out of their energies owing to the existence of that cheap transportation, and therefore they are able to pay greater sums in travel, in commerce and in all that goes to support a system of railways.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Would my hon. friend then disagree with the argument which has been put forward by more than one Minister of Railways in my hearing that the bad results on the Intercolonial Railway are in part due to the fact that it has to contend with competition by water carriage?

I would not agree with that if the line of railway paralleled for any great distance the line of water communication, for instance from a terminal point, a competitive point. If there was a circuitous water route the population along which did not contribute to the traffic of the rail-Mr. CONMEE
way, then the water-traffic would no doubt come into competition with the railway and perhaps injure it; but if the railway parallels a water route anywhere closed where the same community can contribute to both systems, I contend that the world's history ' shows that such railways are the best paying railways. It is so in Europe. The railways paralleling the Danube, which is the cheapest water channel of carriage in Europe, are the best paying systems of railway on the European continent. A very eminent authority in the United States, Mr. Lyman E. Cooley, one of the most eminent engineers in that country, stated in my hearing that the people of the United States would be paid for the investment they made in the improvement of the Mississippi river, even if not a pound of freight was carried on the Mississippi. It may be that the railway is a more convenient means of transportation, a more convenient utility than the vessel route, but he made this statement, and I think it was fully justified, that the river was there as a regulator to bring down the combination of the railways in case they charged too much, and he said it was not alone the interest upon the capital that was to be considered, but that the improvements saved to the producers of the Mississippi valley $100,000,000 a year in their freight and passenger traffic. I do not think the argument advanced this afternoon as to the possibility of the line between Moncton and Quebec being unremunerative is one that can be well maintained. It has not been borne out by history. I do not know of any case in which the building of a new line has been unremunerative, either to the company or to the people of the district traversed by the railway. Generally speaking, these lines of railway have proved successful.
My hon. friend asked about the Intercolonial Railway. I have my own view about the Intercolonial Railway. My opinion is that in the early days of the Intercolonial Railway and during the term of office of the political party to which he belongs that party was not faithful to the Intercolonial Railway. They allowed other systems of railway to rob it of the traffic which it should naturally have. Instead of reaching out for that traffic as a business firm would do if managing the railway, they allowed other systems of railway to tap its territory and draw away from it that traffic which should have been secured for it and brought to it by the business management of the government of the day. I am not saying that either of the two Liberal governments have been absolutely Tight in all their policy in reference to the Intercolonial Railways, but I do say that the loss and the deficits upon the Intercolonial Railway today and throughout its entire history lie entirely at the door of the Conservative party under the leadership of Sir John

A. Macdonald. That is my opinion, I give it for what it is worth. They did not manage it as it should be managed. It is said: 'Why could not the government manage a railway as well as a company?' Where has any government managed a railway as well as a company? It has not been our experience. Neither political party has been able to make a success of the Intercolonial, and I think for very obvious reasons. We did not carry out the scheme to its full extent. It should have been extended to competitive points, it should have been started from a business standpoint and not from a political standpoint. We have not reached the millenium yet; and I am afraid that even if my hon. friend the leader of the opposition was in power, surrounded by the best men he could choose, and he was still operating the Intercolonial, he would have to adopt a much more radical policy than any government has yet adopted, or he would find the Intercolonial pretty near as unremunerative as it is to-day. Of course the country is developing, and it may do better. But I want to point out that a railway at the distance which the Transcontinental runs from the Intercolonial, will not be, strictly speaking, a competitive line. It will assist and not damage the Intercolonial. That has been the history of other lines in this country. We have had evidence to-day of the character of the country, its value in timber, its value in agricultural lands and in general resources. There is no doubt that these resources will be utilized and give prosperity to that section of the country.
Now, let me give my hon. friend a little bit of history. Both political parties I think were mistaken in their views as to the result of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
I am sure hon. gentlemen opposite will say that the Liberals were mistaken in their policy in regard to that great enterprise. Well, I am not going to say they were not mistaken in some respects, because I think they were; but I do say that the Conservatives were mistaken, and very grievously mistaken. Let me remind the hon. gentleman of the contention of his leader in the past. During this and other debates a great- deal of importance has been attached to a branch line from the junction to the head of the lakes. It was pointed out that that line would take from the Transcontinental Railway a great portion of the traffic and divert it at the junction and carry it down to the head of the lake. There is no doubt that it will carry down a great deal of traffic from the west to the head of the lake. I admit that, that is what it is built for. Nature has given to Canada a great waterway, the greatest inland water system of any country in the world; of course, our American friends enjoy the same system. But 175i
no other nation, or no other set of nations, enjoy as great inland waterways as these two countries enjoy. Therefore, it is quite natural that there should be a great deal of traffic to and from the head of navigation. Now, when the government of hon. Alexander Mackenzie proposed to build the Thunder Bay branch, that is the line between Port Arthur and Winnipeg, it was opposed by the Conservatives, it was opposed by the leaders of the hon. gentleman.
I am not sure whether the hon. gentleman was then a member of this House. But I propose to make a quotation from the debates of that time. A strong attack was made on the government because of the proposition to build what is now the Canadian Pacific Railway between the head of the lakes and Winnipeg, and the country was asked to turn the Liberals out of power because they were squandering the people's money in building a portion of the line then called the Thunder Bay branch. But to-day we find our hon. triends calling attention to the great value of the line which this company are allowed to build from the junction to the head of the lakes, the very reverse of their policy at that time. Sir Charles Tupper moved a resolution of want of confidence in the government on that very question. In the debate he decried the expense, he decried the character of the country, and he pointed out that the line if built would be of no value. Their contention was that the traffic from eastern Canada to the west would go through the United States by way of Duluth. Here are the words of Sir Charles Tupper:
But suppose the works to be built, what then? Does any one assume that with a railway from Duluth to Red river a single ton of 'freight would be carried by that route?
That is the Thunder Bay branch. Now, that was the prediction of a great political leader, a man of a great deal of force, one of the men whom hon. gentlemen opposite look up to, and one of the men, I say, that bears a high reputation for ability, for good judgment, for public enterprise throughout the whole country.
Was not the proposition of the Mackenzie government a line part rail and part steamboat, being a different proposition altogether from an all-rail route?

No, that was not the proposition. In the discussion to which I refer there was such an issue as my hon. friend mentions, but it had no reference to that proposition. Sir Charles Tupper was contending for a main line running away north, nearly where the Transcontinental line now runs practically in the same section of country, and would not go to the head of the lakes at all. When a business company got hold of the enter-
'. Oh.

I mean that they are not responsible for the actions of their

party in the past. During my late election this very question came up, and as I say now I said to the people in the good city of Fort William: If there is a Conservative in this city that will stand up in this meeting and show his face to his fellow townsmen and endorse the policy of the Conservative party as regards the bargain with the Canadian Pacific Railway, I will buy him a new hat. I gave the history of the Conservative government in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway and how they failed to protect the rights of the people in controlling rates and there was not a man there who would stand up and endorse that policy. I believe there is to-day not a man on the opposite side of the House, except perhaps one or two, who will stand up and approve of the policy of his leaders in the past. He must condemn them for the improvident bargain they made, and when that bargain is compared with the bargain made by this government which retains not only the ownership of the railway, but the control of the rates on the main trunk system, still further clinches the advantages of that system to the people of Canada by connecting it with the Grand Trunk and its branch lines, and its lines extending to every important city and town in the land and to every manufacturing centre, and building up the prosperity of the country-when, I say, the contract with the Canadian Pacific Railway as compared with this contract, the contract the Conservatives made with the Canadian Pacific Railway is a poor thing indeed.
Did not the Hon. G. W. Ross, now senator, approve of the policy of the Conservative party and compliment them on their foresight in constructing the Canadian Pacific Railway?

He may have done so. I have myself congratulated Sir John Macdonald upon some of his policies. I think he was a great Canadian, I think he did some good things for the country, but I say that in the bargain he made on behalf of the people of Canada with the Canadian Pacific Railway he was not faithful to his trust, or he had not that business capacity which he should have had in the position he occupied. If Senator Ross congratulated the Conservatves, I am sure he did it upon some other ground than the matter we are discussing here to-day. Now, I have nothing more to say further than that there will be no hesitation on my part in giving my hearty support to the policy of the government in this regard. We on this side of the House are not filled up with suspicion; we have confidence that this government is anxious to make the very best bargain it can for Canada, and, that while not imposing impossible or too onerous conditions upon the company they will Mr. CONMEE.
at the same time protect the interests of the people of Canada.

There can be no doubt that the leader of the opposition, since he has once more obtained a seat in the maritime provinces, has been anxious to let the House and the country feel that he is somewhat interested in the development of trade through our national ports. But the solicitude of the hon. gentleman on that point is worthy of a short examination. I think my hon. friend the leader of the opposition would have done much better service for the eastern provinces if he and the gentlemen who support him had seen to it, that in the course of these debates they had not on every possible occasion intimated that the construction of the eastern section was a fatal mistake. If the policy of the opposition party to-day is that the eastern section of the Transcontinental Railway should not be built, then it is wholly inconsistent and beside the question for the hon. leader of the opposition to attempt to mislead the people down by the sea by saying to them that though they opposed the construction of this railway altogether, they have offered a resolution which means nothing in particular so far as creating further obligations upon this company when they operate the road. If my hon. friend and his party were sincerely desirous of adopting a Canadian policy which would enable the eastern provinces to share in the progress of this Dominion as the years go by, and become more and more the means by which the developed trade of western Canada is to flow to the nations across the sea, then my hon. friend and his party would be standing strongly by the proposition that the eastern section of the Transcontinental Railway should be built. My hon. friend knows the provisions contained in the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. All that was threshed out in this House some six years ago when the proposal was first brought to the attention of parliament. My hon. friend knows, and the country knows, that as a result of the views which the government held, and which led them to consider this proposition for the development of Canadian trade through Canadian channels, the government incorporated in the agreement which they made with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company conditions so ample, definite and clear that my hon. friend has not been able to improve upon them in the slightest degree by any resolution which he has submitted to this House then or since. Conditions were,' embodied in the contract, which bind the company, once the railway is operated by them, to carry out the intent of the government in relation to this important project; and it might be well to

place on record just where this government stood on this question six years ago, and where they stand to-day by those conditions. Section 42 of the agreement provides :
It is hereby declared and agreed between the parties to this agreement that the aid herein provided for is granted by the government of Canada for the express purpose of encouraging the development of Canadian trade and the transportation of goods through Canadian channels. The company accepts the aid on these conditions, and agrees that all freight originating on the line of railway, or its branches, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall, when destined for points in Canada, be carried entirely on Canadian territory, or between Canadian inland ports, and that the through rate on export traffic from the point of origin to the point of destination shall at no time be greater via Canadian ports that via United States ports, and that all such traffic, not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper shall be carried to Canadian ocean ports.
That is the kernel of the proposition which led to the incorporation of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, the making of this agreement, and this whole programme. If my hon. friend's policy had been adopted we would have had no line of railway touching Canadian Atlantic seaports at all. We would have a line of railway built from North Bay to Manitoba and westward, which would bring the grain trade of the western country down to Lake Superior. Not a pound of grain nor a dollar's worth of the trade developed in western Canada would reach the Atlantic ocean if my hon. friend's policy of 1903 had prevailed, and if his policy of to-day were carried into effect, and my hon. friend knows it. Therefore, what is the use of misleading the people in this matter? I desire to emphasize the disparity between the hon. gentleman s policy and that of the government on this question. My hon. friend's resolution proposes that there should be effective provision by the Grand Trunk Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Company to fulfil the conditions of the agreement. My hon. friend does not venture to submit to the House what he understands as effective provision. I submit that there is in the agreement an express and definite covenant, which is so clear that there could be no difficulty about its enforcement in a court of law. It binds the Grand Trunk Pacific Company to see that all traffic not specifically routed otherwise by the shipper, shall be carried to Canadian ocean ports. But that is not all. The next section of the agreement renders this condition still more definite and more clear, because it provides:
The company further agrees that it shall not, in any matter within its power, directly
or indirectly advise or_ encourage the transportation of such freight by routes other than those provided, but shall, in all respects, in good faith, use its utmost endeavours to fulfil the conditions upon which the public aid is granted, namely, the development of trade through Canadian channels and Canadian ocean ports.
Now, our friends opposite who have discussed the proposition before the House have a very peculiar attitude. After lamenting and bewailing the necessity for the aid which this government is to give to this company, after decrying the enterprise, after intimating that a colossal debt has been placed on this country as the result of carrying on this enterprise, after endeavouring to lead Canadians everywhere to believe that because the government entered into this project they have placed on the necks of Canadians a burden which i3 going to bear them down for many years to come, these hon. gentlemen will tell you that they are not opposed to the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. Why do they say that? They say that because they have gone to the country twice in the attitude of opposition to this project. They went in 1904, talking about this government going into a reckless enterprise, building a railway through a country about which nobody knew anything, and injuring the credit of Canada by pledging her to millions of expenditure, without any knowledge ot proper investigation of the subject. They received the answer of the people in 1904, and they received it again last year. . My hon. friend from East Elgin (Mr. Crothers) digressed a little this afternoon to indicate that the people of this country did not know what they were voting on. If they did not know what they were voting on in 1904, then our hon. friends who sit on the left of the Speaker must admit that they made a very poor attempt at presenting what th^y called a great big issue when they went before the people at that time. All over this country they had but the one song to sing. More especially was this the fact in the central provinces. Ihey declared that this government was engaging recklessly in the enterprise and asked the people to turn them out, and we had a statement to the effect that if the Conservative party had come in power in 1904, they would have cancelled the contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific. Yet the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Crothers) has the termerity to say that the Canadian people never voted confidence in this government or project. We heard the same remark last year. Whenever an enthusiastic Conservative supporter or orator was tired talking scandal, he reverted to the theory that this government was perpetrating a tremendous wrong in building this

eastern section, that they should only have built from North Bay to the west; and my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, with his friends who sit behind him, coming from the smaller provinces by the sea, were willing to forego all the hopes and aspirations of these provinces to share in the great development which is bound to follow the completion of this railway, if they could obtain some other portions of Canada to support the theory that the Transcontinental should begin at North Bay and go to the west and never reach either Quebec or the eastern provinces at all.
At six o'clock, House took recess.

There was no such understanding, I deny that most emphatically.
On what pretense was the Bill left over if that was not it?

The hon. gentleman is perhaps better able to answer that than I am, I do not know exactly. The hon. gentleman made a request and pledged their honour that if the Bill stood over then when it came up again in regular order it should go through without factious opposition.

Now we must await Mr. Whitney's reply and see whether it is favourable or unfavourable. I think the Bill should not go on to-night until we receive that reply, in accordance with that understanding.

At one time I would have been amazed at the remarks made by the hon. member for Thunder Bay and Rainy RiveT (Mr. Conmee). With the qualifications that have been read by the hon. member for Halton we accepted the proposition of the hon. Minister of Finance. We had a little obstruction I will admit for about five minutes yesterday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Only five?

I do not think it would exceed five. I hate to take up time, but we were allowing a discussion to take place between the hon. member for Rainy River and the hon. Minister of Finance, and during that time I undertook to interest the House with a few pertinent remarks for five minutes or so. I was talking to keep the ball rolling. Then the Minister of Finance said:
As we are not likely to make much progress on the present lines, and as I understand the suggestion to he thav, in view of the objections raised by the Prime Minister of Ontario, there should be several days delay to enable him to present his views, I am prepared to accept that suggestion provided that assurance is given that the matter will then be dealt with without further difficulty according to the discretion of the House.
And then I made the remarks already read. My point is that the suggestion of the Finance Minister was that there should be a delay of several days, not until tonight, because that of course would serve no useful purpose, and as soon as the reply comes from the Ontario government. I have no desire it should be delayed. I do not think there will be any undue opposition, and we will endeavour to present our views when the time comes in as concise a way as we possibly can. It would be idle to think of discussing this matter to-night. We could discuss it but it would not be in accordance with the agreement come to and would be only waste of time.

I would call the attention of the committee to the fact that this Bill has stood over on many occasions. It has stood over now nearly all session. The session is drawing to a close and if the Bill is to become law it has to go to the Senate. I do not think any good purpose can be served by making any further pretense that the Bill is to stand over on the understanding of last evening, because I made this remark after the remarks that have been read by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson). Mr. Blain had asked:
Would not that be good ground?
Meaning that if the Ontario government objected it would be good ground. My reply was:
It may be in the opinion of my hon. friend, but not in the opinion of other hon. gentlemen. I am merely saying that I do not understand the arrangement in that way, and I want to know if it is so understood across the House,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not so understand it. Hon. gentlemen might feel as strongly as they do now on the subject, but I do not understand they would consider it a ground for delaying the matter in order that it might be dealt with in a reasonable time.
Then the discussion was continued. I spoke particularly to the Minister of Finance and asked him if any objection would be taken to the Bill when the next order for private Bills came up on Tuesday and his answer to me was that unless hon. gentlemen permitted this Bill to go through without unnecessary discussion or delay they would be breaking faith with him. That was his reply to me, and that is my reply to the request for delay to-night.
May I ask my hon. friend to explain the paragraph immediately above the first paragraph, the one that was read by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson).

I did say in that paragraph :
I understand from what the Minister of Finance and other gentlemen have said that it is not to be assumed that if the reply from the Ontario government is unfavourable that is to be made a ground for further opposition.
What does that mean?

That simply means that there would be no misunderstanding, that if hon. gentlemen chose to say that because the Ontario government is not favourable to this Bill, we are bound in honour not to allow it to go through.
Does not that answer by my hon. friend mean that we are to wait until the reply from the Ontario government has reached us?

Not at all. What a piece of humbug that would be, with the letter of the Ontario government in the hon. gentleman's possession. We had this answer from the leader of the House last night, stating that if the Ontario government had taken that ground, after knowing the amendments to be made, he would take issue with them. Let me ask the hon. gentleman what good purpose is to be served by this procedure. They cannot expect me to give way further, I think I have done all that is reasonable. They cannot expect me to allow the Order Paper to be cleared and put myself in a worse position than I am now. We have had a discussion, hon. gentlemen have put themselves on record,

there is no mistake about thir position. I think they have said all they are able to say. Let me remind them that the system of our government is that the majority rules. Hon. gentlemen cannot serve any good purpose, either for themselves or for any other interest they choose to champion, by going further than they have gone. If they consider that this measure is not in the public interest they have a right to challenge it by vote. I do not think they have any doubt but that a majority of this House is in favour of it.

I wish to make my position clear, and I think the position generally on this side of the House. There was a distinct understanding between the two parties that this Bill was to be left over in order that communication could be had with the Ontario government. My hon. friend made his own statement in the House when this matter was up for discussion, and he- has qualified it by saying that, no matter what the reply of the Ontario government would be, it would not be a ground for delaying the Bill unnecessarily when it came up again for discussion. I am not going to plead with my hon. friend or with the House not to take up the Bill, if the hon. gentleman wishes to press it. If he thinks it is in the interest of his Bill and in the interest of an early prorogation, to press the matter to-night, he has that privilege, and from this side there will be no complaint. But I want my hon. friend and the House to understand that when we make an agreement between the two sides of the House, we intend "to live up to it. Communication was made with the Ontario government by the first mail after this understanding was reached, and there has been no time to get an answer. As my hon. friend from South Simcoe has said, as soon as that answer is received in respect to the proposed amendment, then on this side of the House we will be prepared to discuss the question, and to finish the discussion, and mv hon. friend can divide the House on the Bill if he wishes.
