speechtext: House resumed debate on motion for the third reading of Bill (No. 128) to authorise a loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific.- Mr. Fielding.

When the House rose at six o'clock, I was endeavouring to point out the very anomalous position occupied by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, in the amendment he has proposed on the third reading of this Bill. I ventured to point out some reasons why, without being at all unfair or unkind to that gentleman, every man who would like to see the com-
Mr. CONMEE
mercial independence of Canada established might well be suspicious of tbe motives which actuate that hon. gentleman. When one recalls that six years ago the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite was opposed to building a railway from one end of the country to the other or constructing a transcontinental line which would have connections with the sea-board at both ends of Canada, when we recall that hon. gentlemen opposite proposed to build, not a transcontinental line, but a line beginning at North Bay and stretching from the western country to the Pacific ocean, thereby absolutely excluding any ocean ports on our Atlantic coast, I repeat that those who want to see the commercial independence of this country asserted might well be suspicious of the motives of the mover of the resolution we are now discussing. Do you find that these hon. gentlemen, after the lessons they must have learned from the two last elections as to what are the views and aspirations of the Canadian people, have abandoned the position they took six years ago and accept the policy that we should have a national line from sea to sea. Is that their position to-day? If it were, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition, might be supposed to have some faith in the proposition he submits. But that is not their position. They stand to-day where they stood six years ago. They still declaim against the absurdity of building what is known as the eastern section and talk about the tremendous burden placed on the people as a result of its construction. Every word they utter is a direct protest against our providing on the Atlantic coast of Canada railway connection by the transcontinental with these ocean ports which we desire to build up and make prosperous. Yet, in the face of that well known opposition of his party, the leader of the opposition, simply because he happens now to represent a constituency down by the sea, endeavours to lead the people to believe, by this resolution, that he is in favour of some effective provision which will aid in the development of our maritime ports.
The policy of my hon. friends opposite in 1903 and 1904 and again in 1909 is a policy of developing trade only and solely through the ocean ports on the Pacific coast. The truth of that position is so clear that it cannot be questioned. Only to-day the hon. gentleman from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) lamented the premature burdening of the people of this country by the debt which was being incurred in the construction of the eastern section of the Transcontinental Railway, without which section none of the traffic of this railway would touch Canadian Atlantic ports. Another reason why I think we have a right

to be suspicious of the candour of hon. gentlemen opposite upon this question is that we have heard them sneer at the position taken by the Prime Minister that it had become imperativelv necessary for Canada to protect herself by having an all-Canadian line in order that our trade might not be dependent upon the bonding privileges accorded to our railways through the United States, privileges which might be withdrawn at any moment with great loss to Canadian interests. The Prime Minister in 1903 asserted that if Canada desired to maintain a position of commecial independence she should at once free her trade fom its condition of dependence^ by haying a line entirely within Canadian territory. Hon. gentlemen sneered at the leader of this government on1 that account and only two years ago, during the discussion of the resolution submitted by the then member for Cumberland, that the advantages of the preferential tariff should be accorded only to imports that came into this country through Canadian ports, the hon. member for East Toronto, a not unimportant member of the opposition declared that the bonding privilege was of the greatest possible advantage to Canada, and that Canada should do everything in her power to preserve that privilege, thus taking the position, to which no objection was raised by the hon. gentlemen around him, that it was right and proper for Canada always to sit under the control of the United States in relation to transcontinental traffic. My hon. friends holding that belief can hardly be deemed to be serious or candid when they talk about providing for the development of trade through Canadian channels and Canadian ocean ports. They are perfectly satisfied to continue a condition under which our trade relations will remain under the direct control of the United States so far as the bonding privilege is concerned. The words of the premier six years ago, that time would not wait in relation to removing Canadian trade from that position of dependency and placing Canada in a position of commercial independence were absolutely true and we are beginning to realize that to-day. Hon. gentlemen who study the position and who recognize the commercial conditions of the country must come to the conclusion that if Canada is to have a future, her commercial independence from the United States in relation to transportation must be asserted, attained and maintained.
Hon. gentlemen opposite have been accustomed to attribute to the right hon. the premier, especially in their partisan newspapers and on occasions when they are free from contradiction, the statement that the Transcontinental would cost Canada only $13,000,000. It was rather refreshing to hon. gentlemen on this side who knew the attitude of some Conservative members 176
and newspapers, and I know it was not pleasant to hon. gentlemen around him, to hear the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Crothers) this afternoon franklv and honestly declare there was nothing in the assertion that the leader of this House had said that the Transcontinental Kailway could be built for $13,000,000. I am reminded that the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) reiterated that statement to-day. I can fairly leave my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) and my hon. friend from West Elgin (Mr. Crothers) to determine which of them is accurate in his interpretation of the Prime Minister's words.
I submit that the policy of hon., gentlemen opposite six years ago and their policy to-day being not to build a transcontinental line but to stop half way across the continent, it is an anomaly for the leader of the opposition to make this motion because if my hon. friends had their way no modicum of trade would ever trickle its way down from the Great Lakes to the Atlantic seaports with such a railway as they proposed. A little might find its way by barge to Montreal or Quebec in summer but for the rest of the year not a pound would reach the Atlantic seaports of Canada. We know their policy in regard to the bonding privilege and we know that the government have wisely provided in the most absolute terms by sections 42 and 43 of the original contract with the Grand Trunk Pacific for the routing of freight by Canadian ports and when we find them asking to have this Bill sent back to the committee to add 'effective provisions' to the Bill binding these companies to the very thing they were bound to do effectively, certainly and surely by the agreement of six years ago we are reminded of the phrase used by the hon. gentleman in his trade policy, 'adequate protection'. I read this afternoon these two sections of the agreement which showed what the government had done upon this question. It is a fair and definite statement. The very basis of the policy out of which grew this transcontinental line was the theory that Canada should develop her trade through her own channels and ocean ports. That is why this government entered into this agreement, that is why the Grand Trunk Pacific was conceived, that is why aid was given to this line and that is why this agreement was made, an agreement which this government propose to carry out. Let me say as one ambitious to see the commercial independence of this country from sea to sea, tnat that commercial independence would not be secured by hon. gentlemen opposite who, by a policy of constructing a railway only half way across the continent, would make the great development of our western country contributory to the



interests of the country to the south for all time to come. I submit further that those of us who are interested in seeing our trade go through Canadian channels and seaports have a right to suspect these Trojan oppositionists who come bearing their gifts. This proposition of our hon. friends might almost be said to have all the signs of a death-bed repentance. After six years of opposition to a transcontinental line intended to develop trade through Canadian channels and Canadian seaports, only one construction can be placed on the resolution of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition if he is candid and honest in proposing it to this House and that is that notwithstanding the declarations made by hon. gentlemen who sit behind and around him, notwithstanding the position adopted by the party during the last six years he has at last come to recognize the merit of the proposition made by tile leader of^ the Liberal party six years ago and to believe that this transcontinental scheme was intended to and will provide for the development of trade through Canadian channels and through Canadian ocean ports. I wish to say in conclusion that I believe that those who have faith in this enterprise, faith in the ideas which prompted it, and faith in its ultimate success, will look to the men who proposed it to implement the promise which is contained in this agreement. To them they will look to see that the conditions in the agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will be carried out. We will expect more from them than we would from hon gentlemen opposite who, if they had their way, would never have built a railway touching any of the Atlantic seaports I believe that where ocean ports are to be developed, where men expect to reap an advantage in the great development which Canada has made, and will make in the next few years, all those interests will regard with suspicion the resolution of the leader of the opposition, and will rely on the leader of this government and the hon. gentlemen who sit around him, believing that their policy will lead to the fruition of the idea which lies at the very basis of this new transcontinental railway.

Or, if he had proposed that when the line is constructed from Winnipeg to Quebec and from Levis to Moncton a grant should he made by the government, or some means should be taken in order to provide a ferry across the river so as to put the Grand Trunk Pacific in the same position that it would be in if the Quebec bridge were completed, then again we would have been happy to have discussed ic with him, because these would have been practical measures which in the end would have inured to the benefit of the maritime ports. But, what did he propose? He proposed that in some way we shall compel the Grand Trunk Pacific to route their height through Canadian sea-ports. Now, let us see what that means. It means that when you get the freight down to Montreal it has to diverge in one of two directions, that it has either to go by the Canadian Pacific Bailway, or perhaps by the Grand Trunk to Sherbrooke and then by the Canadian Pacific Bailway from Sherbrooke to St. John, or it has to go from Montreal to St. John or Halifax by the Intercolonial Bailway. Take either of these propositions and see the absolute ridiculousness of them when you analyse them from the railway standpoint. When a car load of freight from the Bocky mountains or Edmonton, shipped to the sea coast, arrives at Montreal it is handed over to the Canadian Pacific Bailway, or to the Intercolonial Bailway, and then.the Canadian Pacific Bailway, or the Intercolonial Bailway only get their proportionate charge according to the mileage of the whole route. If the Grand Trunk Pacific brought a car load of freight from Edmonton to Montreal and then asked the Canadian Pacific Bailway to transport it from there to St. John on the proportionate mileage, which would figure out according to railway arrangements, why, the Canadian Pacific Bailway would laugh at them. To make it worse, if you asked the Intercolonial Bailway to carry that to the sea-board at that rate, and if that went on for five years, which time might elapse before the Quebec bridge would be available, instead of having an annual deficit of $300,000 or $400,000, you would have a deficit of $4,000,000 or $5,000,000 every year. Yet, that is the proposition which, for political purposes, the hon. gentleman wants this House to adopt. As far as I am concerned, and I speak with a full sense of the responsibility of the position which I occupy in this House as a maritime member, I have no hesitation in saying that I purpose voting against this amendment.
I have no hesitation in saying that, according to my judgment, it does not appear to be a proposition that we should accept, either from the standpoint of common sense or from the railway or any other standpoint. It is only advanced with a political object. It is cnly put up as a scheme by which my hon. friend thinks he can obtain Mr. CARVELL.
some political support in the maritime provinces, but I want to tell him that the people of the maritime provinces have listened to this bogey of the Grand Trunk Pacific too long to be caught by such a shadow as he puts before us to-day. In 1904 the campaign in the maritime provinces yvas fought upon the question of the Grand Trunk Pacific and nothing else. Then the Conservative party did not take the ground which my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) takes now that the road should not be built, but they said that the trouble was that the eastern section from Quebec to Moncton would not be built. They said that it would stop at Quebec, that the government never intended to huild the road from Quebec or that they were building the road to Quebec in order to build up the'port of Portland. Cartoons were published in the papers and circulated all over Canada showing how Portland was to benefit at the expense of Canada. The scheme, according to their contents, never intended to go beyond Quebec. An hon. friend of mine here says that they declared it was not intended to go beyond Gravenhurst. They asked the people to vote for them because the government did not intend to carry out their promise when they said they were going to build the road to Moncton. Now, they have built the road to Moncton. They have built a road the like of which does not exist in Canada to-day. If some of my hon. friends would go over that work, as I have gone over a large portion of it, and look at the character of the work and the grades which they have adopted, they would come to the conclusion that the government at least meant business when they told the people of the maritime provinces that they intended to build the road. The people of the maritime provinces know that it has been built to the ports of St. John and Halifax. They know who have been their friends and who are trying to assist them. The people of the maritime provinces know that the majority of the members of this House who have forced this Grand Trunk Pacific scheme through, notwithstanding the violent opposition of hon. gentlemen opposite, will continue to force it. through and will take whatever means are necessary and wise in order to see that this railway scheme is carried out as it was intended to be carried out, and that Canadian freight is transported over Canadian routes and through Canadian seaports and no others. Having this faith in the Prime Minister- and I am satisfied that the people of the maritime provinces have faith in him and his government-I have no hesitation in voting against this proposition, and I am satisfied that I will be justified' by the great majority of the voters of the maritime provinces in voting against an amendment which is put up simply as a political scheme and not with any honest^desire to

promote the interests of the people of the maritime provinces.

I did not intend to say a word on the motion before the House to-night, but, having listened to the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) and the references made to Nova Scotia I think it would not be fair to the constituency that I represent to give a silent vote on this question. The matte? of this transcontinental railway has been well threshed out, particularly in 1904, when the people of the maritime provinces were instructed to believe that within ft very limited time indeed, long before 1908, we would have the transcontinental railway right down to the city of Halifax and that the province of Nova Scotia would benefit by the road. There was an alternative proposition but I do not propose to delay the House to-night by going into that. The whole province of Nova Scotia was carried in 1904 in the interest of the government and why? Because of the grand and glowing pictures that were painted by the Liberal leaders and candidates as to what was going to happen to the province when that scheme was carried out. The people were deceived to a certain extent and they supported these hon. gentlemen. The result was that we did not have a Liberal Conservative returned in Nova Scotia. In 1904 the hon. gentleman (Mr. Macdonald) carried Pictou by 432 of a majority; in 1908 he carried it by 309, and when he goes back again there is very good evidence that He will not be returned at all, particularly when the people hear the story of the manner in which the Grand Trunk Railway Company has treated the Intercolonial Railway. The Minister of Railways will find that in the maritime provinces the Grand Trunk Railway Company is not looked upon with very great favour. The hon. minister made a statement not very long ago to this House that the Grand Trunk Railway had not treated the Intercolonial Railway very well. He knows that when that notable agreement was made by Mr. Blair between the Grand Trunk Railway and the Intercolonial Railway great things were expected, but I would ask any hon. member in this House whether these great things have been accomplished, or whether the Intercolonial Railway is not in a worse position now than it was when that agreement was made. The people of the province of Nova Scotia do not look with any great hope to what may come to them through the Grand Trunk Railway Company unless the government will undertake to make provision by which the province of Nova Scotia and the port of Halifax will get a fair share of the trade. I believe that there is sufficient trade in Canada for St. John, Halifax, and Sydney
if you like, if we can only get it brought to the east. In 1904 the city of Halifax returned two Liberals and Mr. Roche was elected by 600 majority, but in 1908 Mr. Borden was returned by the handsome majority of 750. Does that indicate that the people of Nova Scotia have very much confidence in this scheme or in the Grand Trunk Railway Company? It certainly does not tend to show that the people of Halifax, who are an intelligent people and who know their own interests, have much faith in the scheme. In 1904, Colchester returned a Liberal with 190 majority, but in 1908 a Conservative was elected with about the same majority. The county of Cumberland in 1904 sent a Liberal to this House with upwards of 700 majority, but in 1908 it returned a Conservative with nearly 500 majority. Does that look as if the peple of Nova Scotia were right in line with this proposition? I have listened to the debates here and there is no doubt in the world that after all the Grand Trunk Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific arc one and the same thing; the only difference being that the Grand Trunk Company dominates the whole business and what the Grand Trunk desires to be done will be done unless the government undertakes to insert such a clause in the agreement as is asked for by this side of the House to-night. In the county of Lunenburg in 1904 the member sitting for that constituency was returned with 451 majority, but in 1908 he could only get 200 majority. The county of Antigonish was represented in the last parliament by a Liberal who had 800 majority but the gentleman representing that constituency at the present time could only get about 20 majority. In Cape Breton South a Conservative was returned in 1908 with a substantial majority, but in 1904 the county was represented by a Liberal whose majority was upwards of 300. The sitting Liberal member for Cape Breton North comes here with a very much reduced majority. A very strong effort was made to get a recount in that constituency and it is now claimed that had a recount been allowed the possibilties are that the gentleman who now represents that county would not be here to-night. In the last parliament Dig-by was represented by a Liberal who had 800 majority but a Conservative represents it in this parliament and his majority was 200.
What about Inverness?

The sitting member for Inverness represents that county as much by the Conservative vote as he does by the Liberal vote, and perhaps if things had not happened as they did happen there might be another story to tell about Inverness, as the hon. member for Inverness knows.
What about Yarmouth?
Well, Yarmouth is an annexationist county and it naturally belongs to the Liberal side of the House.
What about Hants?

My hon. friend (Mr. Black) knows what saved him in Hants and it is not likely he will ever be saved again in the same way. He has nothing to boast about in Hants; his majority is not worth speaking about any how.
I got the largest majority ever given since confederation.

Your turn over from the Conservatives to the Liberals was so quick that some of them did not know you were a Liberal. I want to say, sir, that the people of Nova Scotia and of the maritime provinces generally have no other desire than to see the Transcontinental Railway built. We are not, as the hon. member for Pictou tries to make out, opposing the construction of another transcontinental railway, but we are opposing the extravagant manner in which it is being constructed. We are here to suggest other methods of giving accommodation, and less extravagant methods than the one by which this government is constructing this road. Even though this government may build this road, we demand that it shall be a road for Canada, and Canada alone, not a road that shall have its terminus in the city of Portland. We demand that this government will insert a clause in the agreement that will compel, not the Grand Trunk Pacific, but the Grand Trunk Railway to carry the products of the west down to St. John and Halifax and the other Atlantic ports. What we want is fair play, Canada for the Canadians. That cry is taken up so much by hon. gentlemen opposite that we can hardly get it out first now. There was a time when we did not hear- it so often from them; but now we have to get up pretty early before we can get ahead of some of the men on the other side of the House. That is, when they are voicing the sentiment; when it comes to dealing with the facts and seeing that Canadian products shall go out through Canadian ports, and that foreign goods coming to Canada shall come in through Canadian ports, that is a different proposition. I want to say in conclusion that we in the eastern part of Canada have done all we could, and are willing to do more, to build up the west; we have always sent men to parliament who have been ready to stand behind the great propositions in the interest of Canada. We are to-day as strong as ever in that desire. If Canadian goods ^re exported through Canadian Atlantic ports and imported goods are brought in through Canadian Atlantic ports, the In-

tercolonial Railway will be benefited as well as the whole country. The trouble with the Intercolonial Railway to-day is that it does not get goods either from the east or the west, because it is in a very awkward position, and I am afraid it will continue in that position if the present course is continued. But if we are to have two roads, let us be sure that the trade originating in the west shall come down to Canadian Atlantic ports, so that we shall be getting a fair share of that trade.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. S. LOGGIE (Northumberland, New Brunswick).
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Crosby) seems to have wandered very far from the proposition before the House, carrying us through the political issues in the late contest in many of the counties of his province; but he has not placed before the House any good reason why the amendment moved by the hon. leader of the opposition should be adopted. I wish to make a few remarks on that motion One of its propositions is that we should compel the Grand Trunk Railway Company to route traffic through Canadian channels and Canadian ocean ports, and forbid the diversion routed thereto by the shipper. He has not given us one fraction of evidence to show what power we have over the Grand Trunk Railway Company. We are not, as I understand the present proposition, lending one dollar to the Grand Trunk Railway Company and if the Grand Trunk Railway Company is not receiving anything from this parliament, why should we seek to bind it to do something for us? The hon. gentleman does, however, hold that we should bind the Grand Trunk Pacific Company to carry the traffic through Canadian channels. It is scarcely necessary to remind the hon. gentleman that the Grand Trunk Pacific is already bound by a signed and sealed contract to do so, and therefore it seems to me that placing this amendment before the House on this occasion is, as one hon. gentleman already said, a catch-vote and a vote of want of confidence in the administration. As I understand it, if the principle of the contract, or the amended contract of 1904, had been applied to the prairie section as it was to the mountain section, the Grand Trunk Pacific Company would not be here to-day asking us for a loan. When this project was presented to us, it was expected that the company would bear 25 per cent of the cost of construction; but unfortunately for them, they estimated the cost of the prairie section at about $19,000 per mile, and therfeore asked for a maximum of $13,000 per mile. A good reason has been given why the cost has been more than was anticipated, but because of that limitation to $13,000 per mile instead of

75 per cent of the actual cost, they are here to-day asking us practically to put the prairie section on the basis of 75 per cent of the actual cost. We have been told today by the hon. leader of the opposition that there is imminent danger of the wheat traffic arising in the western provinces being carried to the American seaports, suggesting that it will be diverted at Superior Junction and taken to Port Arthur, thence by water to Midland, and over the Grand Trunk Railway to American ports. To my mind that is the most effective answer to the hon. gentleman's original proposition, that we should aid in building a road to North Bay, and then hand the traffic over to the Grand Trunk Railway. If there is danger to-day of the traffic that goes to Midland being carried on to Portland, would there not be danger of all the traffic that the Grand Trunk Pacific handled for all time to come being handed over at North Bay to the Grand Trunk Railway? Under such circumstances the Intercolonial Railway would become a commercial impossibility, for there would be good reason to fear that all the traffic would go to American seaports instead of to maritime province seaports. Was it not the part of wisdom for this government, when such a proposition was presented to it, to turn it down? My hon. friend is very much concerned about the traffic going temporarily to American seaports because of the unfortunate happening to the Quebec bridge or the non-completion of the road from Lake Superior to the seaboard. The hon. gentleman puts this question to us, but does he show us how that can be done except the Intercolonial Railway forsooth should haul the grain for nothing? He talks about its hauling wheat at two cents a bushel from Montreal to Halifax. But when we realize that two cents a bushel is about four cents per 100 pounds, or $16 for a 40,000 car, we can understand that we cannot successfully manage any great railway with such rates.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I was quoting from the answer given by the government. It is not my statement.

The hon. gentleman was quoting from the answer given by the government, but he must realize that at such rates, we could not carry very much traffic and come out on the right side of the ledger. It is not practical. How could we haul grain 800 miles as against 150 miles? And that would have been exactly the result if the railway had originally gone to North Bay and then have the freight go over the Grand Trunk Railway and the Intercolonial Railway to our maritime seaports. The very dangers which my hon. friend speaks about is the best answer why the government were wise in not adopting
the policy he advocates, and we ought to congratulate the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues on the fact that they _ were sufficiently astute politicians and businessmen not to consent to any such project as was proposed by the Grand Trunk Pacific, namely, to build to North Bay.
Let me now give one or two reasons why it was wise to build the road through the northern portion of Ontario and Quebec, in order that the wheat from our western field should go to our maritime ports. Leaving Winnipeg, we have a railway practically level. A four-tenths grade, I understand, is such that an engine which can start a train on the level will haul it with the same power over a four-tenths grade. Therefore we have a road from Winnipeg to Quebec practically level. We can therefore have grain from the west hauled by rail from Winnipeg to Quebec at practically as low a cost as to Superior Junction and thence to Port Arthur, as you can have it hauled by water to Midland and thence by rail to Montreal. We can deliver it to Quebec by rail at practically as low a rate as we can haul it by the other route and deliver it in the port of Montreal. Again after we get the grain to Quebec, we can send it to our maritime ports. The distance. I admit, is greater than between Quebec and Portland, but what have we to offset that? And that is the pertinent point in having that wheat hauled over the level from Winnipeg to Quebec. When you get it to Quebec, you have placed it very much nearer our maritime ports than if you brought it to Montreal and handed it over to the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Intercolonal Railway. How do you offset the difference as compared with the route between Quebec and Portland? The distance between Quebec and Portland is very much less than between Quebec and our Atlantic sea-board. But we have this to compensate for that difference. Let me give you the words of Mr. Butler, who was at the time the chief engineer of the Transcontinental Commission. In the sessional papers of 1905. we find he tells us that you can haul ten fully loaded trains each way per day on the Transcontinental Railway 486 miles for $2,970,864.54. To -do this same business on the Intercolonial Railway with the 1 per cent grade costs how much? It will cost $5,128,409.06, a difference of $2,157,554 in the operating in one year of ten loaded trains each way per day, and then there will be the difference besides on the passenger freight. What does that mean? We have heard to-day unfavourable criticism on the cost of the division between Quebec and Moncton. I thought that the cost was $30,000,000. but the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) says it will reach $35,000,000. Is not that a profitable investment for the Grand Trunk Pacific? If they have to pay interest at 3 per cent

on $35,000,000, that will amount to about $1,050,000. and they save in operating expenses over $2,000,000, so that they could, by the building of the division between Quebec and Moncton, save $1,000,000 a year over what it would cost them to ship by the Intercolonial Railway, even if they got it for nothing. So that' they will save on operating expenses the interest on the actual cost of the road between Quebec and Moncton.
The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) said to-day, had we not better go slow and not invest quite so much in the section between Quebec and Moncton? I say no, we should hurry along that section and also the section bet-ween Winnipeg and Quebec. My right hon. friend, the leader of the government, says it is our duty at present to hurry on the prairie section. So far as I can see, I say we ought to hurry on every mile of the whole line from Moncton west, and the sooner that is done the better for the transportation interests of this country.
It is not my purpose to take up much of the time of the House, but I thought it my duty to speak on this important matter affecting the maritime provinces. No doubt this resolution of the leader of the opposition will be in the press to-morrow in great headings such as the Conservative^ party conserving the interests of the maritime provinces and the government opposing them. The hon. gentleman is no more earnest in his desire to have the wheat from the western provinces shipped through Canadian Atlantic ports than I and every other hon. gentleman from the maritime provinces. The scheme which he has presented, for the transporting of wheat Tefers only to that which is held over at Midland because it cannot be transported to Montreal before the close of navigation. The question of transport by a martime province port or an American port arises only in connection with winter transportation, and the quantity involved cannot be large, but the benefit that will accrue to our ocean ports when the Transcontinental Railway is completed is incalculable. It is true that a large amount of money is invested in the construction of this road. The leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) said that the net cost of the road to the country on account of interest would be about $13,000,000. As he explained to us to-day, that estimate was based on the cost of the road as then estimated by the engineers, it was not an estimate of cost by the minister but by the engineers in charge. According to the revised estimates we will have a railway of the highest standard from ocean to ocean for a subsidy of about $40,000,000. On all other money which we invest in this road we receive interest, it is as if we got our money

back, put in the bank and drew out interest on it. Comparing this bargain with the bargain for the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway, this seems to me far the better bargain in the interest of the country.
I hope that the hon. gentleman opposite who has proposed this amendment will see his way clear to withdraw it as he could well afford to do under the circumstances. I would commend that suggestion to his consideration.
