speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: Shall the main motion now be adopted?

speakeroldname: Mr. H. B. AMES (Montreal, St. Antoine).
speechtext:
Before the motion is put 1 desire to submit
another amendment of so simple and reasonable a character that it will take but a very few minutes to explain it. This Bill which stands for a third reading provides in its first clause that a loan of $10,000,000 shall be granted to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and that the same shall bear interest at the rate of four per cent per annum. Now I desire to submit to the House an amendment that will provide:
That the rate of interest and charges payable by the company to the government upon and in respect of said loan, should not be iess than the rate of interest and charges which the government should pay in obtaining funds for the purpose of said loan.
As I have said, the proposition I now submit is I think a simple and reasonable one. The Minister of Finance has stated in his introduction that we are to act in the capacity of a banker towards the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and that we are to make them a loan at a stipulated rate of interest. Now if we are to act as their banker, unfortunately we shall ourselves have to borrow before we shall have the money to lend them, and as is well known, when we are borrowing the nominal rate of interest is not all that it costs to secure money. There are other charges as well, and these other charges add no inconsiderable amount to the cost we have to pay to secure the money. So what is known as the average effective rate of interest per unit which takes into consideration all these various costs, is always somewhat above the nominal amount of the loan. I think that if we are to act as banker for this company, and if we must go into the money markets of the world to secure this money, we certainly should ask those who borrow from us to pay us what we have to pay to get that money.
Now the Finance Minister has stated that he expects to be able to borrow this money at a Tate sufficiently below four per cent to cover the cost, so that there will be no money lost on this transaction. If that be the case, then there can be no possible harm in accepting the amendment suggested, and there certainly will be some advantage in passing such an amendment and putting it into the Bill as a precautionary measure. As is stipulated in the Bill, the company will have to pay interest semiannually, and they will not be called upon to pay the first semi-annual instalment until at least six months from the time when the first payment of funds is made to them, and during that period we will obtain the money which we intend to loan to them and we shall have had ample time to calculate what that money will cost us. So by the time the company is first called upon to pay interest there will be no difficulty on our part to ascertain just what that money has cost us, and consequently no difficulty

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance).
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have already discussed this matter at an earlier stage and I do not imagine that anything very new or important can be added to the stock of information in the possession of the House. The hon. member (Mr. Ames) has correctly quoted me as stating that this was a banking transaction-a very proper illustration. If anybody goes into a bank to borrow money he will be rather surprised if the banker should say to him: 'Well, I will lend you this money at four per cent, but if I should happen to have to pay a little more than four per cent I will come back on you for it.' That is not banking business. The banker forms his idea of the value of the money and he fixes the rate which he supposes will coyer his needs. The very first consideration would be that the banker should determine what would be a fair rate of interest. He fixes the rate of interest to his customer, but how he may get the money and what rate of interest he may have to pay the depositor would form no part of the negotiation with his customer; consequently, in fixing a definite rate on this loan, we are certainly acting in accordance with common banking business.
The hon. gentleman is speaking as a banker. Does he imagine for a moment that a banker would lend money at a rate on which he could not possibly gain but would make a loss?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is not the point. I shall come to that in a moment. The question is whether or not there shall be a fixed rate, not what the rate is. That is another branch of the question. My friend (Mr. Ames) is introducing into this question the proposition of an uncertain rate. The point I am making is that the banker would charge his customer a fixed rate. Whether it would be considered a high rate or a low rate is another question. My hon. friend wishes to interrupt?

I do not think the minister has quite read the amendment correctly. The amendment says 'the rate of interest and charges.' The rate of interest can be fixed now by the minister. The minister knows what rate he would pay for his loan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I do not.
Well, he could probably say what rate the company should pay.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
And that the charge for obtaining the loan should be the same charge to the company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The charges are always included in a statement of the net rate of interest. In any statement I make to this House as to what a loan costs I would feel bound to include all the charges in it so as to come as near as I could to what my hon. friend described as the effective rate per unit. The point that 1 desire to make is that when a man goes to a bank to borrow money the banker always makes a fixed rate for the transaction. Whether or not that is considered a high rate or a lew rate, that is another question. I say it is desirable that there should be a fixed rate because we have taken a mortgage as a security,-a security which is desirable to have though not one of immediately great value, and if we are to have a transaction of that character it certainly is desirable that the mortgage should bear a fixed rate of interest and not an uncertain rate of interest. I think, therefore, it is clear that for these various reasons, we ought to have a fixed rate of interest.
Now, in fixing that rate of interest the banker would naturally fix a rate which he believed would be satisfactory to him. He would aim to have a profit. That is the chief business of the banker, but, that is not necessarily our chief business., in the present instance. Nevertheless, it would be the part of wisdom that we should have a definite fixed rate of interest which we might reasonably believe would ooyeT the cost of the money to us and we have fixed that rate at four per cent. My hon. friend assumes that the rate of interest that we will have to pay will be more than four per cent. I have all through carefully guarded this point, and I have given no definite assurance as to what the money will cost. My hon. friend says that I cannot tell at what rate of interest the bonds will be issued. No man can say that in advance. All through this discussion I have insisted respectfully that the proper course for a Finance Minister to take is to hold himself free to issue securities at such time, at such Tate and for such terms as the condition of the money market may require. Therefore, I think it is unwise to found any argument on the assumption that we should have a higher rate. Nevertheless, we should to a certain extent, foresee the conditions of the market. I say there is as much reason to believe that we will make a profit out of this transaction as there is to believe that we will make a loss. I do not think the theory of my hon. friend that we are

likely to make a loss has anything to warrant it. Is there not just as much reason to believe that we may secure a profit? He does not, in moving this amendment, assume that we are going to make a profit. He has no confidence that we will make a profit and he does not say that we must give back to the Grand Trunk Railway any profit we may make. This motion is to no purpose at all. It is based upon the assumption that should the loan cost more than four per cent, we ought to make the Grand Trunk pay more. Why should we do so?
As a precautionary measure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In fixing the rate at four per cent we are taking a reasonable precautionary measure. We are satisfied that the element of risk in the matter is of exceedingly small proportions, of such small proportions that there i# no need practically of our being concerned about it at all. Then I will cite the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The only way you can get over that is by saying that they were wrong. Looking back over the transaction I am not prepared to say they were wrong. I would rather say that they were right. It was wise to fix a definite rate, and if four per cent were not enough, they might have fixed a higher rate, but the fact that they afterwards went to the money market and paid a little more than four per cent will not, in the light of history, be held up against them.
Looking back over the whole transaction I believe it was wiser for the government to fix a rate which they thought would cover the transaction than to have introduced such an element of uncertainty as it proposed to introduce to-day. I do not give that transaction as conclusive evidence but I do say that it is of some value in presenting to the House my argument. I would rather believe that what was done in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway was a fair and reasonable transaction, than that it was an act of imprudence on the part of the government of the day. My hon. friend (Mr. Ames) went away from the loan and he told us that we are going to receive only 3 per cent from the Grand Trunk Pacific on the lease whereas we will have to pay a higher interest rate. That is true, and to that extent we are undoubtedly doing something for the company. Six years ago when the transaction was negotiated 3 per cent was thought to be the fair value of money, but money has since increased in cost and we shall probably find that we may have to pay for some considerable time more than 3 per cent. In that respect we are giving something to the Grand Trunk Pacific. But there are a great many things the government are not giving to the Grand Trunk Pacific. They are not giving them $25,000,000 cash or Mr. FIELDING.
25,000,000 acres of land anywhere in''this Dominion ; they are not giving them miles and miles of completed railway which cost the Dominion many millions of dollars ; they are not giving them exemption ; they are not giving them any of the favours which were lavished upon the Canadian Pacific Railway. When my hon. friend says that we are giving the Grand Trunk Pacific some slight advantage on the interest rate, I would ask him to remember that the Grand Trunk Pacific is far froip. receiving the spendid liberal grants that were given to the Canadian Pacific Railway years ago, and that we are giving to this Transcontinental Railway less, immensely less, than was given to the other corporation by our predecessors in office. Then my hon. friend says that before we lend money we must be sure that we are losing nothing, and that we will at least have our loan returned. The hon. gentleman does not seem to think kindly of this loan to the Grand Trunk Pacific, but as a representative of the great city of Montreal he is interested in the fact that we are lending money liberally to the harbour commissioners of his city, not at one-eighth per cent less than we pay for it but at one and one-eighth per cent less, if I take the same basis that he applies to this case. The hon. gentleman has told us that we are paying four and one-eighth for some money lately borrowed, and I can tell him that we have been occasionally lending money to the Montreal Harbour Commissioners at 3 per cent. What then becomes of this principle that if we are to lend money we must be sure we are to lose nothing ? The Harbour Commissioners of Montreal and the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, are all public bodies interested in the development of the trade and commerce of this country. On what principle do we grant a subsidy to a railway and receive not one cent back?
Can the harbour commissioners of Montreal make a profit in the operation of its works in the same way that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company will make a profit put of their line?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am delighted to have the assurance of my hon. friend that the Grand Trunk Pacific is going to make a profit.

The Minister of Finance has great imagination. I did not say the Grand Trunk Pacific would make a profit,
I merely asked as to the possibility of the Harbour Commissioners making a profit out of their works in the same way as a railway company might.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
Then what is the object of the comparison?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: When we grant a subsidy to a railway company does that company make profit for the government or profit for themselves? When we grant a subsidy to a railway company we get our return in the development of the trade of the country.
Does the Minister of Finance see no distinction between a railway company that operates a public service for profit, and a harbour commission which operates a public service as a trust?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Of course they 'are serving the public in a different way. But the policy of the Dominion of Canada has recognized the fact that a railway company is interested in developing the trade and commerce of the country and that in granting aid to that railway company and not getting a cent back, we are getting our profits through the development of the commerce of the country.
I know the Minister of Finance wants to be perfectly fair; will he allow me one word?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Certainly.

There is one essential difference between the Grand Trunk Pacific from Winnipeg to the coast and the harbour of Montreal. The railway line is the property of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company while the harbour of Montreal is the property of the Canadian government and every dollar spent on Montreal harbour is spent on the property of the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have already said there is a distinction, but all these corporations are serving the country although in different ways and by different means. As a matter of principle I say that every railway in this country is recognized by the parliament of Canada as a public corporation serving public interests, and were it not so upon what ground could the payment of a single dollar in subsidies be justified? Whether it be the Canadian Pacific Railway, or the Grand Trunk Railway, or any other railway that comes to this parliament for aid, we never look upon it as a personal transaction for the individual gain of somebody, but in every case it is considered a transaction associated with public interest, and for the sake of the public interests and not for the saae of private gain we grant aid in one form or another. My hon. friend (Mr. Ames) will see at once that if we apply to the Montreal Harbour Commission the rule that in lending money we must first provide that we shall lose nothing, then, the great works which have been successfully carried on in the harbour of Montreal and of which my hon. friend I am sure is as proud as I am, would never have been completed. The hon. gentleman
(Mr. Ames) further said that the government had no right to lend money to anybody unless it had money to lend. Again that rule would be unsatisfactory if applied to the Montreal Harbour Commission, because we have advanced money to that body when we did not have it in our treasury. It was, however, a proper obligation on us to assist such a great public work and we borrowed the money when the necessity arose as we will have to do in this case. We are assisting an enterprise in which this parliament feels a warm interest, because it is one closely identified with the progress and development of the country. We have granted aid to assist that enterprise, but small aid in comparison with what was granted to the other company in former years; and in granting this loan we do not consider that we are giving the Grand Trunk Pacific Company any great favour at all. We are looking after the credit of the Dominion as much as after the credit of the Grand Trunk Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. They could go out and get this money, as their bonds have a commercial value; but we feel that if they went on the market and forced the sale of those securities, they would have to accept a price which would be most unfortunate for the enterprise and would diminish the funds for the construction of the railway. Therefore, in view of the fact that the interests of this great enterprise are so closely blended with the general interests of the Dominion, any sacrifice of the securities of these companies would be a misfortune not only to the companies themselves, hut to the credit of the Dominion. For all these reasons I am satisfied that this loan is no great favour to these companies, but is a fair and reasonable business proposition. We are much more likely to make a profit than a loss so far as our mere interest is concerned; but above all that we are assisting one of the great corporations of the country to carry forward one of the greatest works ever undertaken in the history of the Dominion.

I do not intend to occupy the time of the House more than a few minutes in an effort to set the Minister of Finance right. The hon; gentleman puts this transaction on the footing of a banking transaction in order that he may fix the rate of interest, and the transaction is put in such a shape that the country can never by any possibility make a profit on it, but may lose. That is what he calls a banking transaction. I doubt whether the hon. gentleman could enter the office of any bank in this world and convince the manager that that was a banking transaction. I take it, so far as the debate has gone, that the country desires to make this loan; but I have yet to learn that the coun-

try either wants to make a profit or desires to make a loss. The hon. gentleman seems to think that because he calls it a banking transaction, it is absolutely essential to put in the contract a fixed rate of interest. Well, I have had, not the experience of the hon. gentleman, but something like a quarter of a century of experience in dealing with some such loans on a smaller scale, and I have never yet heard that there was the slightest difficulty in arranging with a bank for a loan at variable rates of interest or for variable charges according to the conditions of the market from time to time. Whv should there be any difficulty in our helping this Tailway company by making an advance of millions to them and saying to them :	' We desire to make no
profit out of you, but we want you to sign a contract that what we pay you shall return to us.' Is there any mystery about a banking transaction that stands in the way of that? Why, Sir, millions of dollars have been loaned on a contract by which the borrower agreed to pay the current rate of interest from time to time to the Bank of England plus i per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In this case there will be only one transaction, and that at the moment when the loan is made.

It is going to be a pretty long contract if you are looking forward to getting your money back. There was not the slightest difficulty in the Finance Minister going to the company and saying :
' We can borrow this $10,000,000 cheaper than you can; we can get the money on better terms; we want to make no money out of you; all we ask is that what we pay you shall return to us, and even then you will make money by it, that is a banking transaction. It is just as simple as a large railway company going to a bank in London and saying. ' We want $2,000,000 from you, and we will pay you from time to time until we repay the loan at current rates month after month or quarter after quarter, plus i per cent of profit to you.' That also is banking, just as much as if there was a fixed rate. The Finance Minister could have done the same in this case, except that the country does not desire that the government should make a profit out of the transaction. We do not ask for i per cent more than the cost, but we do say that we should not be asked to pledge the credit of this country by borrowing $10,000,000 at a time when it requires all we can do to get all that we need for ourselves, without getting back every cent that it cost us. That is all that we ask. But the hon. gentleman is so wedded to the expression banking transaction that he thinks we must not get back all we advance, but he must agree to a fixed rate and take all the risk of loss without any chance of profit.
Amendment of Mr. Ames negatived on the same division.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. S. MIDDLEBRO (North Grey) moved:
speechtext:
At the next meeting of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, which probably was held a few days ago, no doubt they were authorized to issue a large proportion of this $25,000,000 stock, and if they are going on the market with that stock the probability is they will be in the market just as soon as the Finance Minister in his efforts to raise the proposed loan of $10,000,000, so I think the argument that this loan was given to the Grand Trunk Pacific in order to obviate the necessity of going on the market falls to the ground because the company are themselves going into the market for loans probably larger than this one. The right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has alluded to the amount of the security given by the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the object of my resolution to-night is, if possible, to increase, at least to some extent, the amount of the security which we are to get from the Grand Trunk Pacific. I am sure that no hon. gentleman ip this House can object to the Grand Trunk Pacific giving us more security if they can get it." If they honestly intend to repay this loan, they could have, no legitimate'excuse for not giving us such other and further security as they themselves possess. What can we get from them, what do they own? The first point I touch on is in connection with the Lake Superior branch of the Grand Trunk Pacific. As we all know this branch runs for about 198 miles from the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific to the towns of Fort William and Port Arthur. That branch line has been financed without any assistance whatever, except the ordinary railway bonus, from the Dominion government, and in what shape are they? They have financed that branch and to-day it is practically running and in operation. As the hon. gentleman from Rainy River (Mr. Conmee) said, that will be one of the most lucrative portions of the branch lines of the Grand Trunk Pacific-and it will be the more lucrative because of the fall of the Quebec bridge. Owing to that disaster we know that for many years to come the grain from the west will necessarily have to go by that route, so that this branch line will have the carrying trade practically of all grain from the west that cannot be carried by other railways. In what position is that branch line? It received a railway subsidy from the Dominion government of $1,209,-. 000; it received a subsidy in cash from the provincial government of $378,000; it received from Fort William and Port Arthur, or one of them, $300,000 in cash and $50,000 to assist in building a bridge, or $350,000; in all it has received from Dominion, provincial and municipal authorities, $1,937,000, practically $2,000,000 in hard cash. In addition to that it received from the Ontario government 675,000 acres of land, which I value at $2 an acre, making $1,350,000 the value of that land. Thus alto-Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
gether it has received from the Dominion, provincial and municipal authorities $3,-
287,000.	In addition to that, surely the Grand Trunk Pacific or those behind it, the Grand Trunk, have put some of their own money into that institution. There must be a very valuable. equity in the Lake Superior branch of the Grand Trunk Pacific; upon the admission of the Finance Minister there is no doubt that a large proportion of the stock in the Lake Superior branch of the Grand Trunk Pacific is held by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and it is only right, when .this company is asking this government for $10,000,000 more, that they should give us what little security they can in the Lake Superior division. That is along the line of my resolution.
I come now to the Grand Trunk Pacific Townsite Development Company. This company was instituted in order to take from the Grand Trunk Pacific Company something which legitimately belonged to that company in order to take the cream of the institution and put it in the hands cf a; private company. We find the directors of that company are Charles N. Hays, with two shares, $200; E. J. Chamberlin, with two shares, $200; William Wainwright, with two shares, $200; W. H. Biggar, two shares, $200; E. M. Fitzhugh, two shares, $200. In all these directors of that company have ten shares upon which they paid $1,000. The company is incorporated at $5,000,000;	$3,000,000 of this is paid
up and has been issued. Who owns the balance of that $3,000,000? Of the 30,000 shares of the stock issued, ten shares have gone to the directors, who are also the directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific and intimately connected with the Grand Trunk. Ten of these shares belong to them and the remaining 29,990 belong to the Grand Trunk Pacific, and why should not we, when the Grand Trunk Pacific own 29,990 shares in that company say to them :	' If you intend to repay this loan,
give us an assignment or a mortgage on the 29,990 shares.' They have 78,000 acres of land, a large proportion of which is in townsite. They own 86 townsites between Winnipeg and Edmonton and we do not know how many more they will own between Edmonton and the coast. I quote an extract from a pamphlet issued by the Grand Trunk Pacific in November:
The Grand Trunk Town and Development Company (Limited), a majority of the capital stock of which i9 held by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company

And when they say a majority they mean 29,990 shares out of 30,000.
-has acquired land for 86 townsites, between Winnipeg and Edmonton, which have been subdivided into lots and placed on the market for sale; there has been an interest displayed in these townsites most gratifying to the

company, and thousands of lots have already been sold. Thriving towns are springing up where a few months ago there was nothing but the bare prairie; grain elevators, warehouses, dwellings, stores and other evidences of remarkable activity are presented immediately following the laying of the track. The growth is especially astonishing at the division points or terminals of which there are five between Winnipeg and Edmonton, namely:	at Rivers, Manitoba, Melville, Watrons
and Biggar, Saskatchewan, and Wainwright, Alberta, and there are many other towns which given promise of notable development.
As the construction of the railway prpceeds westerly from Edmonton, townsites will be established along the line, and these will be on the market in 1909.
Hon. gentlemen will see that these town-sites are not worth more than $2 or $3 an acre except for the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and were it not for the assistance of the government which has contributed practically nine-tenths of the cost of the construction of that road, those townsites would be practically valueless. Is it not right and just that they should give to us as security what legitimately belongs to the Grand Trunk Pacific in respect of the increment which should go to the Grand Trunk Pacific if these town-sites had been allowed to remain under the control of that railway where they properly belonged. When the Grand Trunk Pacific come to us for a $10,000,000 loan we should say: You, as the Grand Trunk Pacific Coni-pany own 29,990" shares in that townsite company. You have the control and you can, if you will, and you should give to us a mortgage upon your interest in the Townsite and Development Company. In addition to this they own three-quarters of the townsite of Prince Rupert and we all know that in the course of a few years their interest in Prince Rupert will bo worth probably millions of dollars.
In addition to that they have the Grand Trunk Pacific Telephone Company. Wherever a profit is going to be made out of the transactions of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company there is some subsidiary company to reap it. We have the Grand Trunk Pacific Telegraph Company, and in a prospectus relating to it, the Grand Trunk Pacific Company say:
The Grand Trunk Pacific Telegraph Company was incorporated by Act of parliament, 1906, with a capital stock of $5,000,000, for the purpose of constructing a telegraph system along the Grand TrunkJPaoific Railway. The company has broad powers and may establish, construct or acquire by purchase, lease or otherwise, and may maintain and operate any overhead, underground or cable line or lines of telegraph or telephone, or any system of wireless telegraphy, &c.
You have there the telegraph company, which the gentlemen who belong to the Grand Trunk Pacific also control and operate by a separate corporation. Now we say 177
that these institutions, if not the telegraph company, certainly the other two companies which the Grand Trunk Pacific control, should be pledged to this government as security for this loan. We find that the Grand Trunk Pacific has been shorn of all these necessary adjuncts which enable it to be translated from a supine vertebrae into a useful, healthy and legitimate corporate *entity capable of earning a decent livelihood. That being the case, we, say the mortgage should contain a provision creating a lien upon the assets of these other two companies which the Grand Trunk Pacific itself controls. So far as I can see, there is no logical reason why the Grand Trunk Pacific controlling the interest of these two companies should not pledge them to us as further security for the loan. We desire to get all the security we can; we desire to get this transaction placed as near as possible to that of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company loan of 1884 for the purpose of making it to the interest of the Grand Trank Pacific to pay back this loan. One of the reasons why the Canadian Pacific Railway Company paid back the loan was because we had an undoubted security of $200,000,000. The Finance Minister himself admits that as a direct security the mortgage which we are getting from the Grand Trunk Pacific is practically worth nothing, because there are ahead of us three other prior mortgages. So we are in the position of getting a fourth mortgage which the minister himself practically admits is valueless, and we fall back then upon the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. As I said before, I do not place so much value upon the Grand Trunk Railway Company's guarantee, as the government do, because according to admission we have $121,000,000 of mortgage bonds which form the first mortgage against the Grand Trunk ahead of us; we have $19 000,000 rentals capitalized ahead of us, and we have this Bill passed this year for $12,000,000 more. The Grand Trank are issuing these bonds to the extent of $12,000,000 which will also be a prior charge to the present guarantee. That is to say we have directly ahead of us $152,000,000 on the Grand Trunk guarantee. But that is not all. According to the figures brought down by the Finance Minister, the Grand Trunk Company has already guaranteed $30,000,000 more to other creditors and that $30,000,000 more stands exactly in the same position as we do with respect to the present $10,000,000 guarantee. So we have $152,000,000 of direct mortgage security ahead of our Grand Trank Railway guarantee and the $30,000,000 guarantee standing side by side with the present guarantee. So I ask hon. gentlemen, in view of these figures, do they not think it is right that the Grand Trunk Pacific should hand over



to us as further security the interest in these two other companies, which interest they control. I have therefore much pleasure in moving:
That the order of the third reading be discharged, and that the Bill be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House with power to amend the same by providing that the security to be taken and held by the government for the proposed loan should include a mortgage covering the interests of the company (a) in paid-up stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Townsite and Development Company; and (b) in the branch line from Port Arthur to the main line of the National 1 ranscontinental Railway; subject, however, to any charges or liens now outstanding there-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My objection to the motion of my hon. friend is that, in the judgment of the government, which we respectfully ask the House to confirm, there is abundant security for the loan of $10,000,000 which is proposed by this legislation. I think I should not be wrong if I stated that there has never been any loan transaction made by this government in which we had such good security for our money. My hon. friend refers to the alleged securities, which he says were worth $200,000,000, put up in one form or another by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. My hon. friend must know at once that if they could have realized $200,000,000, or one-tenth of that sum on these securities, they would not have come to the government for help at all. The value of any security is the immediate value; the value of any security is the value you can realize upon it in the markets of the world. Though these securities proved themselves in the end to be of great value, it was self-evident that if they had been of great financial value at the time, the company would have raised the money in the money market, and would not have come to the government of Canada at all. It is perfectly evident that at the time the Canadian Pacific Railway Company produced these securities they had little or no substantial value; therefore as a security for the time being they are not worthy of the commendation that "y ho?, friend awards to them. Ultimately they did become valuable, ultimately the loan was paid back. But if we look at the transaction as it occurred at the time the loan was made, it is quite evident that if these securities had had any substantial security in the money market, the company would have raised the money on the money market and would not have come to the government of Canada at all. So in that sense the securities were not valuable, and the government did not have proper security for its money. The government loaned the money upon the faith that the country would be improved, the government loaned the money upon the faith that Mr. MIDDLEBRO.
the Canadian Pacific Railway Company would prove a success, and happily that expectation proved correct. But as a money security, as a market security, as a banking transaction, the securities which they put up had no substantial value 'Comparatively speaking, because if they had, the company would not have been obliged to aPPly to the treasury of Canada.
Now turn to the security we are putting up. I put aside the question of the mortgage which, as I have said, while it is of value for the future, has no immediate value. I do not attach great importance to it, but I hold that we have the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. My hon. friend speaks of the immense amount of securities of the Grand Trunk Railway Company. I shall not follow him in that, I gave the figures before, showing that after all these securities were provided for there was a surplus in the Grand Trunk Railway Company's affairs which would have abundantly protected this loan; and the later reports of last year's transactions confirm that statement and make it even stronger than I did. But we need not go into the question of the value of the securities. The money market watches all these things, and the value of a security can be found at almost any time in the financial journals. But the point I desire to call attention to is that these securities have a financial value, they have a eomnrercial value, they have a value fixed by the men who know how to value these things. All the securities outstanding are well known, all the obligations of the Grand Trunk Railway Company are well known, all the guarantees are well known, and in face of it all the money market fixes the value on securities of a similar character. In the 'Economist' of the 24th April I find that the four per cent bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, issued for the prairie section and which bear the guarantee of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, are quoted at from 92 to 94. That is the value of this class of bonds in the money market to-day. That is the value on the counters of the bankers in London. Cut off a small percentage to represent the difference between an ordinary quotation and what they would receive for a large issue, and I would be justified in stating that you could take these $10,000,000 of bonds, go to any reputable banking house and perhaps get 90 cents on the dollar to-dav. What is the use of talking about having no security for this loan? The most that can be said is that we take the risk of a margin of possibly 10 per cent. Any man who knows anything of the history of the Grand Trunk affairs, any man who knows the standing of the Grand Trunk in the money markets of the world, will say at once that, when we have for

our security the Grand Trunk guarantee, which is quoted in the money market at from 92 to 94, it is preposterous to assert that this government have not an excellent security for this loan.
My hon. friend has had a good deal to say about the town sites. He wants to know about the town sites. At an earlier stage of this discussion several hon. members on the otheT side of the House had a good deal to say about rake-offs, about some individuals getting a profit out of this. We were told that individuals were skimming this business and making money out of it for their personal profit. No attempt has been made to sustain any charge. It was suggested that in connection with the Town Sites Company there were some individuals who were making money at the expense of the company. My hon. friend now says that the stock of the Town Sites Company, a subsidiary company, is held by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company of Canada, and therefore my hm. friend will see that the suggestions offered at an earlier stage of this debate that some individual officials of the Grand Trunk Railway Company were making money privately out of this trans, action were entirely unjustified. The Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company have formed a Town Site Company for purposes which are entirely legitimate. We were told that the government had given them a great deal of land. The government sold them that land at $3 an acre, but we reserved a quarter interest in the profits of the Town Site Company, a fact which my hon. friend has not mentioned at all. There is nothing in any transaction between the Grand Trunk Pacic Railway Company and the Town Sites Company that any one can say is not perfectly legitimate and fair. There is nothing in any transaction between the government and the Town Sites Company but is fair and proper and in the interests of the Dominion.
Did the hon. gentleman ask the Town Site Company to give us security for this loan, their interest in that company?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No. I think that when we have got a security of $9 out of $10_j)f the highest mercantile value, it is nonsense to ask them to give us other security. And then reference has been made to the common stock. The common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company to-day has little or no commercial value. There is some $25,000,000 of it, but if any hon. gentleman can get. possession of it and if he will take it to any of the banks and ask them to loan him one per cent of the whole amount I do not think he can get the money. It is worth substantially nothing at the present time. The stock of a new railway company has no immediate commercial value. Its value de-1774	.
pends on the future. Its value depends on the enterprise. It would be no good to us to-day as a security, and if at any time, by the development of the enterprise, that common stock becomes valuable, we do not want it as a security because it cannot be worth anything until the obligation of the Grand Trunk Pacific has been met. If then, by the development of the enterprise, this common stock becomes of value, at that moment our loan and every other debt against that enterprise will have been fully protected. Believing then that we have abundant security for our loan, better security than a government usually gets, and immensely better than we got in the case .of the Canadian Pacific Railway, I have to ask the House not to agree to my hon. friend's amendment.
Amendment (Mr. Middlebro) negatived on the same division.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance objects very strongly to asking this company for any further security but I have a suggestion to make on lines which have already been discussed and an amendment to propose which, I think, will probably meet the views of the hon. gentleman and of the several members of the government. The Grand Trunk Railway Company own a large quantity of the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. In the Act passed in 1903 it was provided that the Grand Trunk Pacific should take and pay for this stock as it was needed and hold it all. The right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) said that time that every dollar of the money that was received for this common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific would be used in the construction of the railway. It was for the purpose of enabling the Grand Trunk to receive some common stock for which they were to put up some money for the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific that provision was made in 1903. This, however, did not suit the Grand Trunk, or the Grand Trunk Pacific and in 1904 they came again to this parliament and got a change made in the Act by which the Grand Trunk Pacific were allowed to issue to the Grand Trunk common stock as fully paid up stock, not in return for cash or money, but in return for services to be Tendered to the Grand Trunk and especially for a guarantee of Grand Trunk Pacific bonds. The Grand Trunk guaranteed these bonds and now they find themselves unable to float these bonds on the London market at a satisfactory price and they therefore come to this government and ask them for this loan. Do the Grand Trunk at the same time offer to give back this common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific which they have received in return for their guarantee? Not

at all. They propose to keep it all the same. What I am going to suggest in regard to this stock will not hurt anybody, *will not hurt the Grand Trunk or the Grand Trunk Pacific. It will simply protect us in case this loan of $10,000,000 is not repaid. Every hon. member of this House knows the difficulty there is in foreclosing a mortgage when a large enterprise fails. There is always a lot of trouble about it and it takes a long time. If we got the common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific transferred to us in the meantime it would relieve us of all this trouble in case the mortgage had to be foreclosed. The Act provided for the guarantee of the government on a so-called first mortgage, and for the guarantee of the Grand Trunk on a so-called second bond mortgage. But they really were on a par with each other and it was provided that if there is a default in the payment of either of these issues of bonds _a receiver shall be appointed.
The duty of the receiver is to pay, first the working expenses, and after that to divide pro rata any surplus he may have between the holders of the first and second mortgage bonds so called. I would like to see any such difficulty avoided. It seems to me this is a most unwise provision in the original. Act and that we ought to try to safeguard ourselves against similar trouble in connection with this loan. I suggest that the Grand Trunk Bailway Company should transfer to the government all the common stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific at present in its possession. I do not suggest this as a security, for the Minister of Finance is perfectly right when he says that the stock has no value at the present time. But I ask that it be transferred in order that we may have it in our possession in case of default in the payment of these bonds. At the same time provision would be made so that the voting power in this stock should remain with the Grand Trunk Company so long as there is no default in the payment of bonds or interest. What I suggest is a simple precaution to protect the people of the country. The government are the trustees of the people of Canada, but it would seem that the arguments advanced by government supporters have all been in favour of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Bailway Companies, and that the interests of the people have been lost sight of. I enter my protest against the evident desire on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite to make the people of the country believe that we on this side of the House are in some way opposed to the completion of this Grand Trunk Pacific Bailway. Difference of opinion did exist when the original scheme was brought before- parliament, but it has been sanctioned by the people and Mr. PERLEY.
we quite realize that the road must be completed as promptly as possible. The amendment which I offer will not in any way interfere with the credit of the Grand Trunk Bailway or the Grand Trunk Pacific. It will still allow the voting power on the stock and complete control of the railway, so that when the $10,000,000 is paid back the stock will be transferred to the present holders. In case of default, however, the government will have the common stock in their possession and they will be able to assume the road subject to the other liens on it without process of law and without all the trouble which would otherwise be necessary to assert their rights. I beg to move:
That the order of the third reading be discharged, and that the said Bill be referred back to Committee of the W hole House with power to amend the same by providing that all tho stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company in the control of the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall be conveyed and pledged to the government, to be held until the amount advanced has been repaid with interest, but subject to any necessary or reasonable provision as to power to vote on the said stock in the meantime.
Amendment of Mr. Perley negatived on the same division.	,

I have also an amendment to offer, but before making any remarks directly bearing on that amendment, I shall say a few words with reference to the construction work on the Grand Trunk Pacific, particularly in western Canada. I do not conceive that at this ilate hour it would be proper for me to take up the time of the House at length. The matter which I wish to bring to the attention of the House in the first place is in regard to the nationality of the individuals to whom the money of this country has gone in connection with the construction of that line in the west. For some two years this has been a burning question, in the west. On the 22nd of March last certain questions were put to the Minister of- Railways by the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton) on this very subject, and I quote from ' Hansard ': '
Mr. Sifton-by Mr. A. H. Clarke-asked:
1.	What is the total number of employees upon the operating staff of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway above the rank of brakemen?
2.	Of the total number how many are British subjects, and how many are citizens of the United States?
3.	What is the total number of employees upon the engineering staff of the Grand Trunk Pacific, exclusive of labourers?
I. Of the total how many are British subjects, and how many are citizens of the United States ?

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
1. The information to answer this question is furnished by the vice-president and geuer-

al manager of the Grand Trunk Pacific Bailway, as follows: Total number of men above the rank of brakesmen, is 135.
2.	It would seem to be impossible to secure information as to the nationality of the men mentioned without making a complete canvass from Edmonton to Prince Rupert, where many of the employees are in practically inaccessible locations at this time of the year.. The correspondence indicates that it would take at least three months to get the information. It is also stated that 90 per cent of the employees referred to are British subjects or have been residents of Canada for from three to ten years, this assertion being based on the March pay-rolls and from information at hand.
3.	231.	. .
4.	Answered by Number 2, in addition to which it is stated that the following are British subjects: Second vice-president, chief engineer, bridge engineer, freight traffic manager.
And so on through a list of about 15 officials. The House will observe that in these answers the government announced to the country that the percentage, so far as they can estimate, of the operating staff of that road west of Lake Superior, above the rank of brakeman, is 90 per cent of British subjects, that the same figures apply to the engineering staff and that in addition there are two others whom they state are British subjects as well. It would appear from the statement of the department that in the whole list of the engineering staff given only two are British subjects.
speakername: Hon. GEO. P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals):

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext: Will my hon. friend allow me to point out that the statement of the department is not the department's information, but is information furnished to us by the company.

I hope my language could not be interpreted as challenging the bona fides of the department or of the minister in the statement he gave. I do, however, wish, on such information as I have, to challenge its correctness. The answer to the second part of the series of questions is particularly subject to challenge. The engineering staff of the Grand Trunk Pa'cific in western Canada, from what information I have, and I venture to say that it is very complete, is practically dominated by American citizens. To say that 90 per cent of that staff are Canadian citizens is to say what the Grand Trunk Pacific authorities, who furnished that information, could not possibly have had reasonable grounds for asserting. There has been furnished to me to-day, and I can give it to the House, a list of 56 employees of that road, of whom the great majority are engineers; the list is furnished by a gentleman who is an engineer himself and who has been connected with the Tailway; and of those 56, no less that 40 are citizens of the United States of America. In
the list which has been furnished to the Minister of Railways, numbering those on the engineering staff at 231, the company have doubtless taken advantage of the question as put to include in that number those far down in the grade, such as chain-men, perhaps servants, and other employees in minor capacities. Among those who receive the larger remuneration on the railway, the complajnt is very prevalent, and has been for some time past, throughout the western country, that a very decided preference has always been given to citizens of the United States over citizens of Canada. If there were not civil engineers, architects and others of kindred professions actually idle on the streets of Canada today, and competent men at that, this state of affairs would not be so bad. But, Sir, there are highly trained, competent and tried civil engineers idle on the streets of western Canada to-day, and I am informed and believe that the systematic policy of this company is to leave these engineers and give a preference to citizens of foreign lands. There is a double objection to that in this case: In the first place, because the road is being financed practically and entirely by the Dominion of Canada; and, secondly, because the conditions prevailing in this country are peculiarly suited and peculiarly well known to Canadian engineers trained in this country. Instances could be given where the employment of foreign engineers has been highly detrimental to the interests of the road, where serious mistakes have been made entailing heavy loss, and in consequence heavy liabilities to this country, simply by reason of the fact that the engineers employed were trained under conditions that do not prevail in the northern zone of this continent.
Will my hon. friend be good enough to tell us if he knows of any engineer or architect of repute who is today idle in any city in Canada?
I certainly do. I hope my hon. friend will not be so personal as to ask me the name.
I will push the question harder. I would like to know the name.

My hon. friend, I am afraid, displays a lack of something; the House will have to judge what it is. The system which has resulted in the state of affairs to which I have called attention is known to me in some degree. I cannot say that I know many instances, but I know of more than one. A citizen of the United States, perhaps known to some one high in authority on the road, who is likewise a citizen of that country, writes to the engineering department applying for a

position. The answer is given, out of deference to the provisions of our alien labour law, that it is impossible to employ him in this way, but that if he reports to the city of Winnipeg or somewhere else before a certain individual on a certain date, it is more than likely or possible that he will receive employment. That is a very neat way of getting around the alien labour law. The result has been, as 1 have stated, that a feeling very far from content prevails among the profession in this country, particularly in the western part of the country with which I have some personal acquaintance. Now, I submit, especially at this juncture, when we are called upon to vote more money for this road, that it would not be amiss to inquire where that money is going in this regard. I believe that some three or four years ago Judge Winchester was appointed a commissioner to look into the observance of the alien labour law on the part of this company, and that it was found that serious breeches of the law were committed, or methods of getting around it were employed, by the company.
I believe that considerable improvement took place as the result of that action by the government. I believe from reports that I have received that there exists today a condition of affairs which would justify a repetition of that action.
Having said this much, I shall proceed, very briefly, to a statement of the principles of the amendment which I propose to lay before the House. The government have pronounced, as the outstanding merit of this Grand Trunk project, that it was altogether a Canadian project, designed as set out in the very recital of the contract originally entered into in 1893 to build up and protect Canadian ports. But when a resolution is moved by this side of the House with that object, and that alone in view, it is voted down by the other side and voted down on the avowed reason, as stated by the leader of the government, that another time will come when we can introduce perhaps a clause of that kind, but that time stated by the right hon. gentleman is the very time when this very clause in the contract will forbid its being introduced.
Another pardonable principle submitted as the basis of this proposed loan, is that it is a banking proposition; but when we endeavour to infuse into the Bill some principle of banking, by providing that we shall at least_ not_ lose on the transaction, that proposition is voted down at the instance of the Finance Minister who declares that he has an abstract, theoretical horror of a fixed rate of interest but fails to give us any reason, sound or otherwise, for his invincible repugnance.
And when we endeavour to infuse into Mr. MEIGHEN.
this measure the principle of greater security, as a sound principle of banking, we are answered that we have abundant security. The argument of the Minister of Finance on that point was very peculiar. He instanced the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway, in which it was shown by the hon. member for North Grey (Mr. Middle-bro) that we had $200,000,000 of security on a valuation at that time-not a valuation to-day-for the $30,000,000 we advanced. The hon. minister argued that if the Canadian Pacific Railway had a valuation of $200,000,000 at that time, they would not have had to come to the government of that day for a loan. The very fact, he said, that they were forced to do so argued that the security they had to offer was of no value then in the money markets of the world. But in speaking of the present case, he said we have abundant security. If, however, we apply the same argument to this case of the Grand Trunk Pacific as we did to that of the Canadian Pacific Railway, what is the result? The letter of Mr. Hays, the president of the Grand Trunk Railway, to the Finance Minister practically admits that the company was forced to come to this government for a loan. He said in that letter that if this government did not grant the loan the work would have to stop. Could he more plainly say that he could not get the money any where else? Applying then to that case the reasoning of the Finance Minister in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway, we must come to the conclusion that the security the Grand Trunk Pacific have to offer is not considered good in the money markets of the world. Thus in one breath the Finance Minister argues that the security which the Grand Trunk Pacific has to offer is absolutely good, and in the other that it is no good at all. That is the only logical deduction to be made from his argument.
Aside from that point, I have endeavoured to take the government at their word and infuse the principles of banking into this Bill, but they decline my proposition. They put forward an alternative proposition and say we are in partnership with the Grand Trunk Pacific. Well, I am endeavouring to infuse some of the principles of partnership into this Bill since they reject the principles of banking. One of the principles of partnership is that those who contribute to the capital of a business shall also share in its proprietorship. Surely if there is a cardinal principle of partnership, it is that which is embodied in the amendment I beg to move. In section 26 of the Act of 1903, it is set out that the Grand Trunk Pacific shall be capitalized at $45,000,000, of which $20,000,000 shall be

represented by the preference stock and the balance by common stock, and that the common stock shall go to the Grand Trunk Railway as one of the partners. For that $25,000,000 the Grand Trunk Railway said they would give their guarantee, which unfortunately has turned out not to be worth very much. Still they get that $25,000,000 common stock for that guarantee. And inasmuch as we have to give our guarantee for this loan, as we have to raise the money, why should we not get our share of stock as well as the Grand Trunk Railway? True the $25,000,000 of common stock has already been allotted the Grand Trunk Railway, but there is still $20,000,000 of the preference stock untouched, why should we not have a share in that? Why should we not let the Grand Trunk Pacific have one half of that stock and have the government take the other half, and thereby share in the partnership when we share so largely in the liability. I therefore beg to move, Mr. Speaker, the Mowing amendment:
That the said Bill he not now read a hird time, hut that it be recommitted to a Committee of the Whole with power to amend the same by providing that the Dominion of Canada, in consideration of the financial aid which it contributes o his underaking, shall receive paid up preference stock of the Company to the amount of $10,000,000.
Amendment negatived on the same division.
